The manufacturer states that heating and sintering cycles require tight tolerances because small changes affect material quality and properties, and reports final testing of material and components. [PI Ceramic](https://www.pi-usa.us/en/products/piezo-flexure-nanopositioners/piezo-motion-control-tutorial/tutorial-4-16) provides these process details.

The most important manufacturing implication is that a nominal material coefficient is not a sufficient acceptance criterion for a finished stack. The same source notes that piezoelectric coefficients vary with temperature, pressure, electric field, form factor, and mechanical and electrical boundary conditions. It specifically states that preloaded stacks and lever-amplified systems cannot be described sufficiently by small-signal material parameters, so stiffness, load capacity, displacement, and resonant frequency should be measured on the individual component or system.

Material and supplier controls should include:

- approved ceramic formulation and powder source;
- incoming chemical, particle-size, moisture, and lot documentation;
- controlled binder and solvent formulations;
- sintering profile, furnace calibration, atmosphere, and loading records;
- electrode thickness, continuity, adhesion, and resistance;
- poling field, temperature, duration, and orientation;
- capacitance, dielectric loss, insulation, and polarization checks;
- d33 or equivalent material sampling;
- lot identification retained through assembly;
- formal review before any material, electrode, encapsulation, or process substitution.

A 2026 multilayer lead-free piezoceramic study provides an example of process inspection: tape casting produced eleven piezoceramic layers, and microscopy, SEM, and EDS were used to verify layer thickness and ceramic–electrode contact. Its measured device had approximately \(53\ \mu\mathrm{m}\) ceramic layers and \(3\ \mu\mathrm{m}\) internal electrodes. [The Nature Communications study](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41467-026-72278-y) is a material-development example rather than a production-control standard, but it illustrates the need to inspect internal layers rather than rely only on exterior dimensions.

### 4.2 Control machining and dimensional tolerances

Machining tolerances should be allocated from functional sensitivity, not from what a machine can nominally produce. Critical dimensions include:

- flexure thickness and hinge radius;
- actuator cavity length and parallelism;
- preload-element geometry;
- sensor and actuator datum locations;
- platform flatness and perpendicularity;
- alignment-pin locations;
- cable and utility breakout positions;
- bond-line recesses and contact surfaces.

A sensitivity model can be expressed locally as:

\[
\Delta y\approx\sum_i\frac{\partial y}{\partial p_i}\Delta p_i
\]

where \(p_i\) are part, material, or assembly parameters and \(y\) is a system characteristic such as preload, modal frequency, actuator gain, or cross-axis error. The terms with the largest product of sensitivity and variation deserve tighter tolerance, better inspection, or a design change.

Wire EDM is useful for monolithic flexures because it can produce complex compliant geometries without assembled joints. The 2-DOF platform cited earlier used WEDM to create an integrated steel structure. However, WEDM accuracy must be evaluated together with wire compensation, taper, residual stress, heat-affected effects, surface finish, and post-machining distortion. A monolithic flexure should be inspected by coordinate measurement, optical measurement, or functional stiffness testing rather than by checking only overall length and width.

The preload example from [Yong](https://www.eng.newcastle.edu.au/~yy582/Papers/Yong2016_preload.pdf) demonstrates tolerance propagation. A \(+0.00/-0.02\ \mathrm{mm}\) cavity tolerance and \(\pm0.05\ \mathrm{mm}\) actuator-length tolerance produced a calculated preload range of \(13.8\)–\(19.3\ \mathrm{N}\). That range is a design-level calculation, not a statistical distribution, but it identifies the correct question for production: what measured preload distribution results after actual machining and assembly?

### 4.3 Standardize bonding, assembly, and alignment

Bonding can change stiffness, damping, thermal expansion, creep, and resonance. The process should specify:

- adhesive type, batch, storage, and working life;
- surface preparation and cleanliness;
- bond-line thickness and volume;
- dispensing equipment and calibration;
- fixture geometry and clamping force;
- cure time, temperature, humidity, and post-cure;
- inspection for voids, squeeze-out, delamination, and contamination;
- acceptance criteria for the cured joint.

The bonding thermal budget is especially important for thin-film and multilayer piezoelectric devices. A wafer-level PZT process compared electrode systems after thermal treatment, selected Cr/Au because it caused the least degradation, protected the electrode with \(\mathrm{Al_2O_3}\), and used low-thermal-budget parylene bonding. The fabricated devices retained \(85.91\%\) of pristine remanent polarization and \(94.30\%\) of saturation polarization; elevated temperature caused more severe degradation. [The IOP study](https://beta.iopscience.iop.org/article/10.1088/1361-6382/ae4b4a/pdf) supports controlling thermal exposure and bonding chemistry, although its MEMS process is not a complete isolation-assembly process.

Assembly instructions should define the sequence and the reference datums. A robust sequence commonly seats the structure against hard locating features, installs the actuator without side loading, establishes preload through a compliant or measured element, and tightens fasteners in a specified order. The Yong preload design secured top screws before bottom horizontal screws and used sliding-fit contact surfaces to avoid base rotation and unequal horizontal installation forces.

Fixtures should make incorrect assembly difficult. Useful features include:

- asymmetric locating pins to prevent reversed installation;
- hard datums that do not rely on adhesive position;
- preload stops or load-cell feedback;
- alignment targets for optical or capacitive sensors;
- torque-controlled drivers with tool calibration;
- automatic recording of force, displacement, torque, and cure time;
- replaceable wear components with life limits;
- protected cable routing and strain relief.

An assembly that requires an expert to “feel” the correct preload or alignment is not ready for consistent production.

### 4.4 Measure the completed actuator and isolator

Component inspection is necessary but not sufficient. The finished assembly should be tested under controlled loading and boundary conditions.

At the actuator level, useful measurements include:

- capacitance and dielectric loss;
- insulation resistance and leakage;
- free stroke versus voltage;
- blocked force or force–displacement curve;
- stiffness;
- resonance frequency and damping;
- hysteresis loop at defined amplitude and frequency;
- creep after defined voltage steps;
- temperature-dependent response;
- fatigue or cycle stability where relevant.

At the assembly level, add:

- preload;
- alignment and platform level;
- modal frequencies and mode shapes;
- cross-axis sensitivity;
- cable and utility influence;
- sensor gain and phase;
- closed-loop transmissibility;
- residual acceleration, velocity, displacement, and tilt;
- amplifier current and voltage under representative disturbances.

The manufacturer guidance in [PI Ceramic](https://www.pi-usa.us/en/products/piezo-flexure-nanopositioners/piezo-motion-control-tutorial/tutorial-4-16) explicitly argues for individual characterization because material coefficients do not describe preloaded or amplified systems adequately. The resulting calibration record should not be treated as an optional service document; it is part of the product configuration.

### 4.5 Calibration traceability and measurement-system analysis

Sensor calibration should be traceable to a reference and performed over the actual frequency and environmental range. ISO 16063-21 comparison calibration couples a reference transducer and device under test to the same shaker motion, then calculates sensitivity and phase from their electrical outputs. [ISO 16063-21](https://www.iso.org/standard/27053.html) permits uncertainty evaluation from significant sources, including check-standard results.

A back-to-back calibration arrangement should control:

- common mechanical mounting;
- axis orientation;
- preload and torque;
- cable routing;
- shaker amplitude and frequency;
- temperature and humidity;
- reference calibration status;
- phase and amplitude processing;
- repeat measurements and uncertainty.

A 2025 reference-comparison calibration used a common sensor platform, sinusoidal acceleration from \(10\) to \(1000\ \mathrm{Hz}\), \(0.1\)–\(1g\), \(25\pm1^\circ\mathrm{C}\), and ten-cycle averaging at each point. It reported expanded uncertainty increasing from \(1.7\%\) at \(10\ \mathrm{Hz}\) to \(2.1\%\) at \(1000\ \mathrm{Hz}\), with reference calibration, environmental factors, and repeatability contributing approximately \(60\%\), \(25\%\), and \(15\%\), respectively, at one reported operating point. [The Vibroengineering calibration study](https://doi.org/10.21595/vp.2025.25675) illustrates how an uncertainty budget should identify the dominant contributors instead of reporting only a single accuracy number.

Measurement-system analysis must distinguish:

- repeatability: variation when the same instrument, operator, part, and method are repeated;
- reproducibility: variation due to operators, setups, environments, and time;
- part variation: real unit-to-unit variation.

[Hoffa and Laux](https://dr.lib.iastate.edu/bitstreams/c3a8d337-b12f-4a40-aa68-3f1ff9adc0ff/download) report the AIAG P/T convention that a measurement system below \(10\%\) is generally acceptable, \(10\%\)–\(30\%\) may be acceptable depending on application importance and cost, and above \(30\%\) is unacceptable. These are decision boundaries, not a substitute for engineering judgment. A measurement system that cannot resolve the isolator’s critical variation cannot support a meaningful capability study.

### 4.6 Process capability and inspection strategy

For a stable, approximately normal process with upper and lower specification limits, the common capability indices are:

\[
C_p=\frac{USL-LSL}{6\sigma}
\]

\[
C_{pk}=\min\left(\frac{USL-\mu}{3\sigma},\frac{\mu-LSL}{3\sigma}\right)
\]

\(C_p\) measures potential spread if centered; \(C_{pk}\) also reflects centering. Ppk includes longer-term variation and should not be confused with short-term Cpk. Capability indices are invalid or misleading when the measurement system is poor, the process is unstable, the sample is unrepresentative, or the specification does not describe the true functional requirement.

A worked production example in an APQP guide used 100 consecutive pilot-line samples for a force constant. The example reported \(C_p=1.67\), \(C_{pk}=1.62\), and an ongoing Cpk criterion of at least \(1.33\), while distinguishing an initial Ppk criterion of \(1.67\). It also recommended X-bar/R monitoring and reaction rules for nonrandom trends. [The APQP example](https://ansv.net/en/posts/apqp-rd-practice/) concerns a micro-actuator production flow, not a completed vibration isolator. Its value here is the structure of the method, not the transfer of its numerical capability to another product.

For an isolator, capability studies should target characteristics such as:

- actuator capacitance and resonance;
- flexure thickness and stiffness;
- preload;
- sensor sensitivity and phase;
- assembled natural frequencies;
- cross-axis response;
- amplifier gain and current;
- residual noise;
- closed-loop transmissibility;
- settling time and control effort.

Critical characteristics should be measured on every unit when practical. Sampling can be used for destructive, expensive, or long-duration tests, but sampled qualification does not replace 100% screening of characteristics that can escape and materially affect isolation.

### 4.7 Evidence limits for product-specific manufacturing statistics

The supplied evidence supports the processes, mechanisms, and measurement methods above, but it does not provide a complete product-specific statistical record for a serial precision piezoelectric vibration isolator. Specifically unavailable are:

- lot-to-lot statistics for ceramic coefficients, actuator properties, bonding, and preload in completed isolator assemblies;
- a complete assembled-isolator Cp/Cpk/SPC study;
- target-product environmental and aging validation across production lots;
- product-specific supplier incoming-acceptance data and material-lot records;
- standardized-work and control-plan evidence for a complete isolator build;
- unit-to-unit distributions for system transmissibility, noise, modal response, and control performance.

The strongest supported conclusion is therefore procedural: these quantities must be defined as production evidence, measured with a capable measurement system, and linked to serial numbers. A component-level capability example cannot be presented as proof of complete isolator consistency.

## 5. Control algorithms and nonlinear-error compensation

### 5.1 Begin with a measured plant

Control design should begin with system identification of the assembled structure and its actual electronics. The model should include:

- actuator voltage-to-force or charge-to-force behavior;
- sensor gain, phase, and filtering;
- payload and inertia-block mass properties;
- flexure and mount stiffness;
- damping and structural modes;
- cross-axis transfer functions;
- preload and load dependence;
- temperature dependence;
- ADC/DAC delay and computation latency;
- saturation and current limits.

A useful sequence is to identify the open-loop frequency response at low amplitude, verify modes and cross-coupling, identify nonlinear response at representative voltage and preload, then design and test the controller. Identification should be repeated at significant payload, temperature, and operating-point corners.

### 5.2 Feedback, feedforward, and hybrid control

The major alternatives can be compared as follows:

| Architecture | Required information | Main strength | Main limitation | Appropriate use |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Feedback | Payload, relative, force, or inertial response | Rejects disturbances and model uncertainty | Limited by sensor noise, delay, phase margin, and actuator authority | General-purpose isolation and active damping |
| Feedforward | Coherent disturbance reference, such as floor acceleration | Can cancel disturbance before it appears in payload response | Requires an accurate, causal reference and plant model | Measured floor vibration or periodic machinery disturbance |
| Hybrid feedback/feedforward | Both response and disturbance measurements | Combines model-based rejection with robustness | More sensors, calibration, computation, and failure modes | High-performance active isolation |
| Robust feedback | Plant uncertainty bounds and measured response | Guarantees bounded performance across modeled uncertainty | Conservative weighting and control effort | Variable payloads, cross-coupled multi-axis systems |
| Adaptive control | Online error or plant information | Tracks changing payload, temperature, and modes | Stability, convergence, excitation, and validation are harder | Slowly varying operating conditions or degradation |

Feedback remains the foundation because it does not require a perfect disturbance reference. The 2021 active–passive isolation study explains that feedforward uses a vibration-source reference, while feedback detects residual vibration without needing that reference. It also notes that feedforward generally requires more sensors, which can reduce weight and reliability. [The study](https://www.mdpi.com/2076-3417/11/8/3338) therefore recommends selecting feedback when the disturbance reference is unreliable or expensive to obtain.

Feedforward is valuable when the reference is measured upstream of the payload and is sufficiently coherent with the disturbance. In the active-hard-mount thesis, measured floor vibration was used with adaptive filtered-x least-mean-square compensation. The standard FIR representation required many parameters, while a fixed-pole IIR representation achieved similar performance with fewer parameters and lower computation. Its performance depended critically on the selected fixed poles. [University of Twente](https://doi.org/10.3990/1.9789036530163).

A hybrid loop is often the practical choice: feedforward removes predictable, coherent disturbance components, while feedback stabilizes the plant and corrects model error. The hybrid controller comparison reported three techniques—filtered-x LMS feedforward, LQG feedback, and a combined feedforward-feedback structure—and proposed the hybrid for robust performance and fast convergence. [JSME International Journal](https://doi.org/10.1299/jsmeintmovic.6.1.105).

### 5.3 Active damping and disturbance rejection

Active damping should target the modes that matter to payload accuracy. A velocity-feedback loop can emulate a virtual damper; a force loop can suppress the transmitted force; and a relative-displacement loop can regulate leveling and low-frequency motion. The loop should be placed around the physical quantity that is both observable and causally controllable.

For low-frequency disturbance rejection:

- use absolute inertial sensing when base motion and structural modes are the principal concern;
- use relative displacement sensing when payload-to-base position or tilt must be maintained;
- use force sensing when the transmitted force is the critical output;
- use multiple sensors when rotations and cross-axis motion cannot be inferred reliably from one channel;
- avoid integrating noisy acceleration indefinitely without bias management;
- use high-pass or bias-estimation strategies to prevent integral drift.

A spacecraft isolation study combined a geophone for absolute velocity with a force sensor and used integral force feedback to suppress a hyperelastic resonance peak. It maintained a loaded natural-frequency target of \(15\)–\(25\ \mathrm{Hz}\). In its uncompensated loop, phase margin was only \(1^\circ\); a lead compensator increased it to \(17^\circ\). [The spacecraft isolation study](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10813719/) is a useful warning that an apparently responsive loop can be unstable or unusable until phase margin is deliberately restored.

Disturbance observers can estimate the combined effect of unmodeled hysteresis, force variation, structural vibration, and external disturbance. They are attractive when a detailed physical model is too costly or changes with operating conditions. However, the observer bandwidth must not amplify sensor noise, and its uncertainty bounds must be tested against saturation and delay.

### 5.4 Robust and multi-axis control

For a multi-axis isolator, independent single-axis PID loops are adequate only when the off-diagonal plant terms are sufficiently small. Otherwise, a coordinate transformation, feedforward decoupling, or multivariable controller is required.

A six-degree-of-freedom AVIS study first used feedforward compensators based on modeled off-diagonal transfer functions to suppress mutual interference and then applied mixed-sensitivity \(H_\infty\) feedback. Ground vibration, direct platform disturbance, and compensation error were treated as uncertainty. The design used diagonal feedback channels after decoupling and selected weighting functions from system characteristics. [Nguyen et al.](https://www.mdpi.com/2076-3417/14/17/7966).

The robust-control choice should reflect uncertainty:

- LQG is useful when a linear state-space model and stochastic disturbance assumptions are credible;
- mixed-sensitivity \(H_\infty\) is useful when tracking, disturbance rejection, sensor noise, and control effort need explicit frequency weighting;
- modal or notch control is useful when a small number of well-identified resonances dominate;
- decoupling feedforward is useful when cross-axis dynamics are stable and accurately identified;
- gain scheduling is useful when payload or temperature changes are repeatable and measurable.

Robust control is not a substitute for structural design. If a cable changes a mode by several hertz or preload moves actuator gain substantially, the uncertainty model must include those variations or the production process must reduce them.

### 5.5 Adaptive and predictive control

Adaptation is justified when the plant changes during normal operation and when a safe fixed controller cannot meet the full performance requirement. Possible changing variables include payload mass, payload center of gravity, temperature, actuator preload, ceramic aging, and damping.

Examples include:

- Youla-parameter adaptation with recursive least squares to suppress time-varying deterministic residual vibration;
- model-reference adaptive control with online parameter updates;
- adaptive filtered-x LMS for changing disturbance paths;
- fuzzy or ANFIS adaptation for nonlinear parameter dependence;
- sliding-mode predictive control with an observer for matched and mismatched disturbances;
- online modal or frequency-response estimation followed by bounded gain scheduling.

The adaptive Youla design in [the 2021 active–passive study](https://www.mdpi.com/2076-3417/11/8/3338) used an inner LQG controller to shape the loop near the natural frequency and recursive least squares to tune the free Youla parameter online. The study reports suppression of unknown, time-varying, low-frequency deterministic residual vibration, while noting that the central controller alone could not completely suppress that component.

A 2019 fractional-order robust model-reference adaptive controller adjusted parameters online using fractional proportional–integral adaptation laws and used only measurable plant input and output. Its reported experiments covered a \(20\)–\(500\ \mathrm{Hz}\) band and compared favorably with traditional MRAC in control effort. [The Journal of Vibration and Control study](https://doi.org/10.1177/1077546319875260) provides an example, not a reason to select fractional-order control by default.

A 2025 study applied output-feedback sliding-mode predictive control to an active–passive piezoelectric isolator with variable-mass payloads. A neural-network state observer and generalized proportional-integral observer estimated matched and mismatched disturbances, while receding-horizon optimization used predicted sliding-state information. [Su et al.](https://doi.org/10.1109/TIE.2025.3563717) show how advanced control can address changing payloads, but such an algorithm also increases verification, computational, and failure-containment requirements.

For a product, adaptation should have:

- bounded parameter ranges;
- a known initialization and calibration state;
- excitation limits that cannot damage the actuator;
- a fallback fixed controller;
- lockout conditions for sensor failure or loss of observability;
- logged parameters and adaptation history;
- a requalification plan when the algorithm or update law changes.

### 5.6 Hysteresis and creep compensation

Piezoelectric hysteresis is a memory-dependent difference between increasing and decreasing displacement at the same voltage. It depends on voltage history, amplitude, frequency, preload, temperature, and mechanical boundary conditions. Creep is a slower time-dependent displacement drift after a voltage change.

The 2023 review reports dynamic hysteresis errors of about \(15\%\) in one synthesis of the literature, increasing to almost \(35\%\) at higher drive frequency. The values span different actuators and conditions, so they are not a universal specification, but they establish why open-loop voltage control is insufficient for high accuracy. [Kanchan et al.](https://doi.org/10.3390/technologies11060155) distinguish rate-independent models for low-frequency behavior from rate-dependent models needed at higher frequency.

#### Charge control

Charge control regulates the charge or current supplied to the piezoelectric element instead of relying only on voltage. Because actuator capacitance changes with operating state, charge control can reduce hysteresis and creep.

The principal options are:

- series-capacitor insertion;
- current-controlled charge amplification;
- capacitor-based charge sensing;
- linear or nonlinear charge controllers;
- digital charge amplifiers.

Series-capacitor insertion reduces sensitivity to capacitance variation by a factor \(C/(C+C_p)\), where \(C\) is the inserted capacitor and \(C_p\) the actuator capacitance. The same voltage-divider effect reduces the voltage available to the actuator and therefore reduces stroke unless a higher source voltage is provided. [Kanchan et al.](https://doi.org/10.3390/technologies11060155) describe this direct trade-off.

Charge control is attractive when hysteresis reduction is more important than maximum stroke and when specialized current-sensing hardware is acceptable. It is less attractive when the actuator must operate over a large dynamic range, when low-frequency leakage causes charge drift, or when several axes require closely matched charge loops. Voltage control with model-based compensation is usually easier to productize across actuator types, but it requires calibration and model management.

#### Model-based voltage compensation

Common hysteresis models include:

- Bouc–Wen: differential, relatively convenient to implement, and suitable for rate-dependent behavior when extended;
- Prandtl–Ishlinskii: operator-based, useful for rate-independent or modified asymmetric behavior, with an inverse often convenient for feedforward;
- Preisach: flexible memory representation but more demanding identification and inversion;
- Duhem: differential representation with rate dependence;
- Maxwell–Slip: intuitive spring/friction representation but limited for some high-frequency behavior;
- neural or fuzzy models: flexible, but dependent on training data and validation boundaries.

The model should be selected by required frequency range, minor-loop behavior, asymmetry, computational budget, inverse availability, and parameter stability across temperature and preload. A model with a small fitting error in one open-loop sweep may fail in closed loop if it does not reproduce minor loops, rate effects, saturation, or preload dependence.

The 2021 vertical-pendulum isolator used separate polynomial fits for ascending and descending actuator curves, inverted those models, and combined them with a digital PID adjuster implemented on an FPGA. Its inner-loop model error was less than \(0.042\ \mu\mathrm{m}\) for the tested actuator under stable laboratory calibration. [Wang et al.](https://doi.org/10.3390/app11104526) show the value of a simple model when speed and implementation simplicity matter, but the result is specific to the tested NAC2023 actuator and calibration environment.

High-gain feedback can reduce residual hysteresis and creep without explicitly modeling them. In an AFM piezo scanner, high-gain feedback reduced a measured hysteresis error from \(6.29\ \mu\mathrm{m}\) to \(1.04\ \mu\mathrm{m}\), an improvement of more than \(83\%\), and reduced a 15-minute creep error from \(8.41\ \mu\mathrm{m}\) to \(0.37\ \mu\mathrm{m}\). Further gain increase was limited by gain margin. [Leang and Devasia](http://www.kam.k.leang.com/academics/pubs/LeangKK_2002.pdf) provide these results for an AFM scanner, demonstrating the trade-off between nonlinear-error rejection and stability.

The most robust product architecture is often:

- feedforward inverse hysteresis compensation for the repeatable part;
- feedback for residual hysteresis, creep, disturbance, and unit variation;
- temperature and preload scheduling or compensation;
- individual actuator parameters stored by serial number.

### 5.7 Feedback–feedforward integration

A two-stage controller separates tasks:

1. Feedforward uses an identified plant and inverse nonlinear model to generate the approximate voltage or force needed for the desired motion or disturbance cancellation.

2. Feedback corrects model error, external disturbance, sensor bias, actuator variation, and drift.

[Leang and Devasia](http://www.kam.k.leang.com/academics/pubs/LeangKK_2002.pdf) proposed high-gain feedback for hysteresis and creep, followed by inversion-based feedforward for vibration at high scan rates. They emphasize that feedback provides robustness to model uncertainty while feedforward provides high-speed dynamic compensation.

For vibration isolation, the analogous arrangement is:

- feedforward from a floor accelerometer or geophone for coherent floor disturbance;
- feedback from payload inertial or relative-motion sensors for residual motion;
- active damping around structural modes;
- actuator hysteresis compensation inside the drive path;
- supervisory limits around voltage, current, travel, temperature, and sensor validity.

The feedforward path must be causal. [Beijen et al.](https://doi.org/10.1109/acc.2015.7171051) show that perfect disturbance cancellation is impossible in practice because compensation arrives late, plant inversion is imperfect, controllers are discrete, and sensor dynamics contribute residual error. The resulting frequency-domain waterbed effect means that improving rejection in one band can create sensitivity or control effort elsewhere.

### 5.8 Latency, phase margin, and implementation limits

Every filter and computation adds phase lag. A useful first-order approximation is that a pure delay \(\tau\) contributes phase lag \(-\omega\tau\), so the same delay becomes more damaging as crossover frequency rises.

The control design should budget:

- sensor and conditioner delay;
- ADC conversion and sample-and-hold;
- digital scheduling and execution;
- communication and buffering;
- DAC update;
- amplifier group delay;
- actuator and structural phase;
- anti-alias and reconstruction filters.

The CAVI prototype reported a \(700\ \mu\mathrm{s}\) data-acquisition delay. It used phase-lead and phase-lag action, a \(0.25\ \mathrm{Hz}\) high-pass pole to prevent drift, and a \(100\ \mathrm{Hz}\) low-pass pole to limit high-frequency sensor-noise coupling. High-Q mechanical modes above \(100\ \mathrm{Hz}\) required a notch filter, and the combination of delay, roll-off, and notch phase loss limited high-frequency control. [The CAVI study](https://beta.iopscience.iop.org/article/10.1088/1361-6382/adf0e2) also notes that cryogenic mode shifts can require a different notch frequency and controller design.

Controller verification should include gain and phase margins at each payload and temperature corner, sensor and actuator tolerances, latency variation, saturation, quantization, and loss of a sensor. The controller should be tested both with the nominal model and with measured worst-case plant variants.

## 6. Design-phase management for identical-product consistency

### 6.1 Convert needs into measurable requirements

Consistency begins before the first prototype. Customer or machine-level needs should be converted into a requirements specification with:

- controlled axes and rotations;
- payload mass, center of gravity, inertia, and load distribution;
- floor and internal disturbance spectra;
- residual acceleration, velocity, displacement, and tilt limits;
- frequency bands and transmissibility limits;
- settling time and allowable overshoot;
- sensor noise, phase, and cross-axis limits;
- actuator force, stroke, voltage, current, and temperature limits;
- operating, storage, transport, and humidity conditions;
- service life and cycle count;
- calibration and traceability requirements;
- acceptance statistics and measurement uncertainty.

A requirement such as “low vibration” is not testable. It should become something such as a residual acceleration spectral-density limit over a named band under a defined payload, temperature, floor spectrum, and control state. A requirement such as “identical behavior” should become a distribution of unit-level metrics, a maximum allowable spread, and a comparison method.

An APQP/QFD guide illustrates the conversion of a vague haptic requirement into measurable values: resonant frequency, peak acceleration, rise time, and specified verification instruments. Its numerical example is for a micro-actuator rather than an isolation system, but the requirement structure is directly transferable. [Chen’s APQP example](https://ansv.net/en/posts/apqp-rd-practice/) emphasizes that every requirement should name both a measurable value and a verification method.

### 6.2 Build a requirements and error-budget traceability matrix

Each system requirement should link to:

- a responsible subsystem;
- a physical parameter;
- a tolerance or uncertainty allocation;
- a verification method;
- a test condition;
- an acceptance limit;
- a design record;
- a production control.

For example:

| System requirement | Dominant contributors | Design allocation | Verification |
|---|---|---|---|
| Residual acceleration in a low-frequency band | Sensor noise, floor reference, structural resonance, loop delay | Sensor noise budget, modal placement, controller phase margin | Shaker or measured-floor transmissibility test |
| Payload tilt | Rotational stiffness, center-of-mass offset, sensor alignment, cable torque | Symmetric support, tilt sensor calibration, flexible utilities | Six-axis tilt and cross-axis test |
| Unit-to-unit closed-loop gain | Actuator force constant, preload, sensor gain, amplifier gain | Individual calibration and tolerance limits | EOL frequency-response and closed-loop test |
| Long-term drift | Ceramic aging, adhesive creep, temperature, electronics offset | Material/environmental design and compensation maps | Thermal, humidity, storage, and aging tests |
| Settling time | Structural damping, active damping, delay, saturation | Mode separation, deterministic control, current reserve | Step or load-disturbance test |

This matrix prevents a common failure: assigning a system-level accuracy requirement to a controller team while leaving the largest error source—such as preload or sensor mounting—unallocated.

### 6.3 Allocate tolerances by sensitivity and interaction

Tolerance allocation should be performed on a coupled electromechanical model. Relevant variables include:

- flexure dimensions and elastic modulus;
- actuator \(d_{33}\), capacitance, stiffness, and resonance;
- preload and bond-line thickness;
- sensor gain, phase, and orientation;
- amplifier gain, current, and output impedance;
- ADC/DAC quantization and timing;
- payload mass and center of gravity;
- temperature and thermal gradients;
- cable stiffness and routing.

Use sensitivity analysis to identify which variables materially affect residual motion or stability. Then choose the least expensive effective control:

- tighten the part tolerance;
- redesign the geometry to reduce sensitivity;
- add an adjustment or datum;
- measure and calibrate the parameter;
- schedule controller parameters;
- accept the variation only if the error budget permits it.

Worst-case allocation is appropriate for safety or hard travel limits. Statistical allocation can be appropriate for random, controlled dimensions, but only after process distributions and correlations are known. A Monte Carlo result is not evidence of consistency until it is validated against measured production distributions.

Preload is an example of an interaction requiring coupled analysis. A tolerance that changes preload can change actuator gain, hysteresis, stiffness, resonance, and fatigue simultaneously. Treating preload as an independent scalar error will understate its effect.

### 6.4 Verify the design at component, subsystem, and system levels

A V-model is effective when each development level has a corresponding verification level. [Bartel et al.](https://past.isma-isaac.be/downloads/isma2014/papers/isma2014_0145.pdf) describe a requirements-driven sequence in which contract requirements define component demands, component designs are verified, integration tests check system properties, and final testing validates the whole system against the original requirements.

A suitable verification sequence is:

1. Verify material and actuator properties, including capacitance, insulation, stroke, force, resonance, hysteresis, creep, and temperature behavior.

2. Verify flexure geometry, stiffness, stress, fatigue margin, alignment, and parasitic motion.

3. Verify the amplifier and signal chain with representative capacitive loads and sensor impedances.

4. Verify sensor frequency response, noise, cross-axis response, mounting, and calibration uncertainty.

5. Verify actuator–structure subassemblies with measured preload and production-representative cables.

6. Identify the integrated plant and compare measured modes and transfer functions with the model.

7. Verify the controller in simulation, hardware-in-the-loop, and physical closed-loop tests.

8. Verify environmental corners, payload corners, disturbance corners, and fault conditions.

9. Validate the intended installed use with the actual tool or a representative payload and floor spectrum.

TMC’s product literature makes performance conditional on comparing site floor-vibration data with the tool’s floor-vibration criteria and confirming that the isolator transfer function provides the required isolation. [The STACIS installation guidance](https://www.gmp.ch/pdf/Datasheets/TMC/STACIS%20product%20brochureGMP.pdf) illustrates why design verification cannot stop at a laboratory shaker test with an arbitrary disturbance.

### 6.5 Freeze configuration across hardware, software, and calibration

A precision isolator has several configuration items:

- mechanical drawings and tolerances;
- material and surface-treatment specifications;
- actuator and sensor part numbers;
- amplifier schematic, PCB revision, and component values;
- ADC/DAC configuration;
- FPGA or DSP firmware;
- controller gains and filters;
- nonlinear-model parameters;
- temperature and preload compensation maps;
- calibration fixtures and procedures;
- acceptance-test software;
- serial-number database schema.

All must be revision-controlled. A change to a capacitor, adhesive, sensor cable, firmware timing, filter coefficient, or actuator supplier can change the closed-loop plant. Engineering change review should ask:

- Does the change alter a calibrated parameter?
- Does it change a mode, delay, gain, noise floor, or thermal path?
- Does it affect interchangeability?
- Does it require re-identification or requalification?
- Which existing production units are affected?
- Can units built before and after the change be compared under the same test?

Supplier guidance for piezoelectric OEM programs recommends that the NPI package contain revision references, critical dimensions, performance targets, inspection methods, validation records, pilot-release criteria, and controlled scale-up. It also warns that material substitutions, process changes, tooling refreshes, inspection changes, packaging, and logistics changes may require review and revalidation. [Yujie Piezoelectric](https://yujiepiezo.com/blog/component-supplier-innovation-partner-piezoelectric-transducer-manufacturer/) provides this design-transfer guidance.

### 6.6 Define a calibration strategy before design release

Calibration should not be added after the mechanical and control design is frozen. The design should provide:

- accessible calibration interfaces;
- known reference points and datums;
- sufficient actuator stroke for calibration excitation;
- safe fixtures for blocked-force or displacement tests;
- temperature and preload sensing;
- firmware support for calibration mode;
- nonvolatile storage for unit-specific parameters;
- versioned calibration files;
- recalibration and requalification criteria.

For a piezoelectric isolator, the most useful strategy is often a hybrid of common nominal parameters and individual measurements. Use common model structure and common control laws, but store per-unit values for:

- sensor gain and phase;
- actuator voltage-to-force or voltage-to-displacement gain;
- capacitance and leakage;
- resonance frequency and damping;
- preload;
- hysteresis and creep parameters;
- cross-axis matrix;
- temperature compensation coefficients;
- final closed-loop correction.

A closed-loop piezo system manufacturer states that each delivered system is calibrated for linearity and repeatability, that results are recorded in a calibration protocol, and that the control system must be calibrated with the specific actuator. [piezosystem jena](https://www.piezosystem.com/piezopedia/measurement-systems/) gives a product-level example of this principle and reports a \(0.037\%\) nonlinearity example at a \(157\ \mu\mathrm{m}\) position. The numerical result is product-specific; the configuration rule is broadly applicable.

### 6.7 Transfer the design through a controlled pilot

Design transfer should include:

- a released bill of material and approved supplier list;
- controlled drawings with critical-to-function dimensions;
- process flow diagram;
- PFMEA or equivalent risk analysis;
- control plan;
- assembly work instructions;
- calibrated fixtures and gauges;
- operator training;
- golden sample or reference unit;
- first-article and pilot-build records;
- measurement-system analysis;
- capability data from consecutive pilot units;
- software and calibration release package;
- packaging and transport requirements;
- defined production-release gates.

A golden sample should not be merely the first unit that worked. It should be a characterized, stable reference with known hardware revision, firmware revision, calibration data, modal response, actuator properties, and acceptance results. Its purpose is to detect process drift and distinguish a product change from a test-system change.

The pilot should include time-separated builds and, where possible, more than one material or supplier lot. A process can look consistent when one engineer builds a small group of units under special attention. It must be tested under normal production staffing, tooling, inspection frequency, and takt time before release.

## 7. Production-phase management, testing, and performance consistency

### 7.1 Qualify suppliers and control incoming material

Supplier approval should examine process capability and change control, not only catalog specifications or a successful prototype sample. A piezoelectric factory should be able to show control from incoming ceramic through shipment, including:

- raw-material control;
- in-process inspection;
- final performance testing;
- nonconformance handling;
- batch traceability.

[The supplier-quality checklist](https://www.induinsighthq.com/news/Precision_Fluid/Micro_Actuators/Piezoelectric_Actuator_Factory_Checklist_for_Stable_OEM_Quality.html) recommends these five evidence areas and calls for strict engineering-change control over ceramics, adhesives, electrodes, wiring, and packaging.

Incoming inspection should be risk-based but functionally relevant. Depending on the component, it may include:

- ceramic lot and certificate verification;
- dimensions, flatness, and parallelism;
- capacitance, dielectric loss, and insulation;
- d33 or sampled electromechanical properties;
- actuator stroke, stiffness, resonance, or force;
- flexure geometry and surface condition;
- adhesive batch, shelf life, and storage;
- sensor gain, noise, and calibration status;
- amplifier PCB component and firmware revision.

A supplier sample that passes inspection does not demonstrate serial stability. The checklist warns that pilot units often receive extra care, while serial output exposes actual process capability. It recommends a pilot order with predefined gates for incoming quality, documentation, packaging, lead-time discipline, and functional consistency across multiple lots or time-separated shipments. [InduInsight’s supplier assessment](https://www.induinsighthq.com/news/Precision_Fluid/Micro_Actuators/When_a_Piezoelectric_Actuator_Factory_Becomes_a_Reliability_Risk.html) makes this prototype-to-serial distinction explicit.

### 7.2 Use standardized work and controlled fixtures

The production process should specify not only what to assemble but how to assemble it. Standardized work should define:

- cleaning and contamination limits;
- part orientation and datum sequence;
- fixture identification and setup verification;
- actuator seating and side-load limits;
- preload application and measurement;
- fastener type, torque, and sequence;
- adhesive dispensing and cure;
- sensor alignment and zeroing;
- cable routing and strain relief;
- electronics programming and configuration;
- environmental conditioning before calibration;
- retest and rework rules.

Fixtures should control the variables that are too sensitive to leave to operator judgment. A load cell or displacement-controlled preload station is preferable to relying only on screw torque when preload is a critical parameter. A laser or optical alignment gauge is preferable to visual centering when sensor-axis error materially affects cross-axis performance.

Tool wear should be monitored. Locating pins, nests, cutters, WEDM guides, dispensing needles, torque tools, and calibration references can all drift. The APQP worked example uses a shot counter to trigger locating-pin replacement at 100,000 cycles and an in-line laser sensor to measure a critical air gap. Its \(0.05\pm0.01\ \mathrm{mm}\) air-gap example is for a micro-actuator line, not an isolator, but the prevention-and-detection logic transfers directly. [APQP process-control example](https://ansv.net/en/posts/apqp-rd-practice/).

### 7.3 Monitor process capability with SPC

Statistical process control should monitor both upstream variables and final functional outputs.

Upstream charts may include:

- flexure thickness and hinge dimensions;
- cavity length and parallelism;
- bond-line thickness;
- cure temperature and time;
- assembly preload;
- fastener torque;
- actuator capacitance and leakage;
- sensor offset and gain;
- amplifier output gain and current;
- firmware programming status.

Functional charts may include:

- actuator free stroke and stiffness;
- resonance frequency;
- hysteresis width;
- assembled modal frequencies;
- cross-axis coupling;
- sensor noise floor;
- closed-loop bandwidth;
- residual transmissibility;
- settling time;
- control effort.

X-bar/R or equivalent charts can detect changes in mean and within-subgroup variation. Individuals and moving-range charts may be appropriate when one unit per operation is available. Ppk is useful for long-term performance, but it should not replace Cpk from a stable short-term process. The control plan should define reaction limits, lot containment, investigation triggers, and restart criteria.

The APQP example specifies reactions such as stopping a line after one point beyond a \(3\sigma\) zone, nine consecutive points on one side of the centerline, or six consecutive increases or decreases. These exact rules should be adapted to the actual process and risk, but they illustrate that an SPC chart must have a pre-agreed action, not merely a display.

Capability analysis must be performed on the actual product and production process. The reported micro-actuator example with \(C_{pk}=1.62\) cannot be used to claim that a complete precision isolator has equivalent capability. The isolator’s relevant distributions must be measured after assembly, calibration, and final test.

### 7.4 Maintain serial-number genealogy

Every unit should have a serial-number record linking:

- ceramic and actuator lot;
- sensor and amplifier serial numbers;
- flexure and machined-part lots;
- adhesive batch and cure record;
- operators and assembly station;
- fixture and tool IDs;
- preload and alignment measurements;
- firmware and hardware revisions;
- calibration coefficients and date;
- end-of-line test data;
- environmental conditioning;
- nonconformances, rework, and concessions;
- field failures and corrective actions.

Traceability should be granular enough to distinguish a material-lot issue from an operator, fixture, supplier, or firmware issue. The supplier checklist recommends tracing each unit or lot back to materials, operators, tools, and test results so that failures can be isolated quickly. [InduInsight](https://www.induinsighthq.com/news/Precision_Fluid/Micro_Actuators/Piezoelectric_Actuator_Factory_Checklist_for_Stable_OEM_Quality.html) also emphasizes that deviations should be documented, contained, and permanently corrected.

Calibration data should be stored in a structured database rather than only printed on a certificate. The record should preserve raw measurements, fitted parameters, uncertainty, test conditions, software version, and acceptance decision. If a controller uses an individual actuator model, the firmware should verify that the correct calibration file is loaded for that serial number.

### 7.5 End-of-line acceptance testing

End-of-line testing should combine fast 100% screening with deeper sampled or periodic qualification.

A practical 100% screen can include:

- visual and dimensional inspection of critical interfaces;
- capacitance and dielectric-loss measurement;
- insulation resistance and leakage;
- amplifier voltage and current verification;
- actuator stroke or force at defined points;
- resonance or impedance check;
- preload and alignment;
- sensor zero, gain, and noise;
- short closed-loop response test;
- cross-axis or functional interlock check;
- firmware and calibration identification;
- protection and fault-response test.

A system-level acceptance test should include at least a low-amplitude frequency sweep or modal check, a defined disturbance or shaker test, residual motion measurement, and a step or load-disturbance response. The test should use the production payload or a controlled representative payload, defined cable routing, and known environmental conditions.

The supplier checklist recommends final checks for displacement, force, capacitance, resonance, hysteresis, insulation resistance, and response under specified drive conditions. It also recommends reliability screening for cycling, temperature exposure, humidity stress, and drift after storage or transport simulation. [InduInsight](https://www.induinsighthq.com/news/Precision_Fluid/Micro_Actuators/Piezoelectric_Actuator_Factory_Checklist_for_Stable_OEM_Quality) lists these as evidence of process maturity, but the exact limits and sampling plan must be set by the isolator’s requirements.

The test system itself requires calibration and Gage R&R. If a production laser, accelerometer, force sensor, or shaker has drifted, an apparent unit-to-unit shift may be a measurement-system shift. Reference units and check standards should be tested periodically to detect that condition.

### 7.6 Compare units and lots on common axes

Unit-to-unit consistency should not be judged by whether every unit has identical raw voltage or displacement. It should be judged by whether each unit meets the same functional metrics under the same test conditions.

Use a common test matrix:

- same payload mass and center of gravity;
- same cable and utility arrangement;
- same temperature and humidity;
- same sensor bandwidth and filtering;
- same actuator drive waveform;
- same preload;
- same disturbance spectrum;
- same controller and firmware revision;
- same measurement reference.

Compare:

- mean, standard deviation, range, and distribution shape;
- modal frequencies and damping;
- actuator gain and phase;
- sensor noise;
- cross-axis transfer;
- closed-loop transmissibility;
- residual acceleration or velocity;
- settling time;
- control effort;
- calibration drift.

Separate variation into:

- within-unit repeatability;
- operator or setup reproducibility;
- unit-to-unit variation;
- lot-to-lot variation;
- time or aging variation.

A unit with an unusual but passing result should not automatically be “tuned” into the population. The investigation should determine whether the result reflects a real product difference, an incorrect calibration file, a test setup error, or an emerging process trend.

### 7.7 Environmental qualification, fatigue, and aging

Environmental qualification should reproduce the actual service risks:

- temperature cycling and thermal gradients;
- high and low temperature operation;
- humidity exposure;
- storage and transport;
- mechanical shock and vibration;
- actuator cycling and fatigue;
- electrical overvoltage or repeated high-field operation;
- insulation and leakage after exposure;
- calibration drift after conditioning;
- modal stability after aging.

Tests should be performed at component, subassembly, and product level. For example, ceramic insulation may pass in isolation while a bonded stack fails after thermal cycling because of adhesive mismatch or electrode-edge stress. A flexure may survive static stress but drift after high-cycle operation. A controller may meet room-temperature performance but lose phase margin after a resonance shifts.

A manufacturer reports open-loop motion consistency after more than one billion cycles for one actuator family and a separate test article reaching \(3.22\times10^{12}\) cycles. [The PI/TMC white paper](https://www.techmfg.com/learning/whitepapers/piezo-driven-active-vibration-control-pushes-limits) gives these results as manufacturer-specific endurance evidence, not as a universal lifetime for all piezoelectric actuators. Qualification should therefore use the actual ceramic, encapsulation, preload, drive waveform, environment, and duty cycle of the product.

Environmental tests should also be statistically connected to production. The product-specific evidence supplied here does not provide environmental or aging distributions across production lots for a complete isolation system. The appropriate production control is to define an initial qualification program, repeat it after significant changes, and use periodic sample testing or accelerated life monitoring to verify that production has not shifted.

### 7.8 Nonconformance, containment, and corrective action

A nonconformance process should distinguish:

- immediate containment of suspect units and lots;
- correction or rework;
- root-cause analysis;
- verification of the corrective action;
- disposition of already shipped units;
- update of PFMEA and control plan;
- supplier corrective action where appropriate;
- requalification after a process or design change.

Common failure patterns include:

- an actuator lot with shifted capacitance or resonance;
- preload outside the functional window;
- a sensor installed with incorrect orientation;
- an adhesive cure outside specification;
- a cable that bypasses a flexure;
- an amplifier component change that alters phase;
- a firmware or calibration-file mismatch;
- a test fixture that has worn or lost alignment;
- environmental drift mistaken for product drift.

The corrective-action record should retain the serial numbers, lot boundaries, measured data, containment decision, cause, action, and follow-up capability evidence. A closed corrective action should demonstrate that the relevant distribution returned to control, not merely that one failed unit was repaired.

## Closing judgment

A precision piezoelectric vibration isolator becomes accurate when its sensor, actuator, structure, electronics, and controller are designed as one measured plant. The highest-leverage improvements are usually a low-noise and correctly mounted sensing path, a stable high-voltage actuator interface, a stiff and thermally controlled structure with deliberately placed modes, measured preload and alignment, and a hybrid control architecture that combines feedback robustness with calibrated feedforward and nonlinear compensation.

Consistent products require a second layer of discipline. Requirements must be quantitative, tolerances must be allocated by sensitivity, designs must be verified at system level, and hardware, firmware, models, fixtures, and calibration records must remain under configuration control. In production, supplier and material control, standardized assembly, capable measurement systems, SPC, serial-number genealogy, product-specific calibration, end-of-line functional testing, environmental qualification, and closed corrective-action loops turn a successful prototype into a repeatable product.

# Manufacturing Technology Options for Hollow Motor Shafts in NEV Electric Drive Units

For most high-volume steel hollow motor shafts in New Energy Vehicle (NEV) electric drive units, the strongest default is a near-net cold, warm, or semi-hot forging route followed by precision machining, heat treatment, grinding, balancing, and inspection. A simple, repeatable shaft favors cold or warm forging, extrusion, or tube-based rotary swaging. A bottle-shaped or stepped monobloc shaft with a demanding internal contour favors semi-hot mandrel radial forging; a thin-walled tubular shaft with integrated splines or helical features favors rotary swaging combined with axial forming or spline rolling. No single process can be ranked as universally cheapest or strongest because the supplied evidence contains no common geometry, volume, fatigue, balance, cycle-time, and cost comparison across all routes.

The practical material baseline is alloy or case-hardening steel—especially 42CrMo4/4140, 20MnCr5/20CrMnTi, 20CrNiMo, or, for higher duty, 4340 or 18CrNiMo7-6. Aluminum, titanium, magnesium, copper, stainless steel, and nickel alloys are technically formable through several route families, but the available evidence does not establish them as generally qualified substitutes for high-volume NEV traction-motor shafts. For prototypes and low-volume programs, machining from tube or bar remains the most flexible fallback.

## Roadmap and assessment method

The report first defines the shaft’s operating envelope and the requirements that make the application different from an ordinary industrial motor shaft. It then catalogs the current forming families, separating established automotive practice from technically demonstrated, conditional, and emerging routes.

The comparison addresses four practical questions:

1. Which materials and heat treatments can each process accommodate?
2. How do tooling, capital, cycle time, material utilization, automation, and production volume affect cost-effectiveness?
3. What machining, spline or gear formation, heat treatment, balancing, and inspection remain after forming?
4. Which routes best fit high-volume NEV shafts, and under what geometry, material, and volume conditions should an alternative be selected?

The recommendation is intentionally conditional. The available evidence includes industrial production descriptions, supplier data, standards, simulations, laboratory studies, and analogues such as automotive axle sleeves and transmission shafts. These sources establish process mechanisms and commercial plausibility, but they do not provide one validated head-to-head ranking for a single NEV shaft design.

## 1. Application requirements for an NEV hollow motor shaft

### 1.1 Functional role in the electric drive unit

A rotor shaft is the mechanical link between the electric motor and the reduction gear or final drivetrain. It supports the rotor stack and, depending on motor architecture, permanent magnets, excitation-winding supports, balancing disks, slip-ring or induction components, and bearing locations. In a permanent-magnet synchronous motor (PMSM), the shaft carries the laminated rotor and magnets; in an electrically excited synchronous motor (EESM), it also supports star-shaped disks and field windings; in an asynchronous machine (ASM), it supports the steel core and conductive cage or bars. These arrangements are described in the [Hirschvogel rotor-shaft paper](https://www.hirschvogel.com/fileadmin/user_upload/ATZlive_Paper_HIVO_Rotorshaft_klf_V6.pdf).

The shaft performs several functions simultaneously:

- transmits continuous and transient torque to the gearbox;
- carries bending loads created by rotor mass, gear forces, bearing reactions, and assembly;
- maintains the rotor stack and bearing seats on a common axis;
- transmits torque through internal or external splines, a helical gear, or another formed interface;
- withstands repeated acceleration, deceleration, and regenerative-braking reversals;
- maintains dimensional stability at high rotational speed;
- reduces mass and polar inertia through the hollow section;
- sometimes provides an oil, coolant, wiring, or lubricant passage.

A hollow shaft is therefore not simply a lighter solid shaft. The bore changes torsional stiffness, bending stiffness, local buckling resistance, thermal behavior, wall-thickness sensitivity, and the way manufacturing defects are distributed.

Zhang et al. describe an electric-motor shaft as carrying tension, compression, bending, and torsional loads. Their design discussion also places the first critical speed above the operating speed, with a design target approximately 20–25% higher than operating speed in the cited rotor-attached shaft case [Zhang et al., 2018](https://publica.fraunhofer.de/bitstreams/a343908c-8dd5-4ed6-bcbf-366b0a2a9d09/download).

Regenerative braking adds an important load-direction issue. A vehicle-drive-shaft patent distinguishes mainly one-directional torsion in a conventional internal-combustion drivetrain from forward and reverse torque application in hybrid and electric vehicles during traction and regenerative braking [US20160305469A1](https://patents.google.com/patent/US20160305469A1/en). That patent concerns a vehicle drive shaft rather than a motor rotor shaft, so its load magnitudes and geometry should not be transferred directly. Its mechanism is nevertheless relevant: a shaft designed for repeated torque reversals must be assessed for bidirectional torsional fatigue, spline contact, weld or interface integrity, and residual-stress effects.

### 1.2 Representative geometry

A useful screening envelope, rather than a universal specification, is:

- outside diameter: approximately 40–70 mm;
- wall thickness: approximately 4–6 mm;
- overall shaft length: approximately 200–350 mm;
- two precision bearing sections;
- one or more splines, a gear, or an end-forming feature;
- optional stepped or bottle-shaped inner contour;
- possible internal oil or coolant passage.

These ranges come from professional manufacturing experience summarized by Fink. The same source reports general outer-diameter tolerances of approximately 14–20 μm, bearing-section outer-diameter tolerances of 7–12 μm over the bearing length, and bearing cylindricity of 5–8 μm for high-speed rotor shafts [Hirschvogel rotor-shaft paper](https://www.hirschvogel.com/fileadmin/user_upload/ATZlive_Paper_HIVO_Rotorshaft_klf_V6.pdf). They should be treated as representative production ranges, not as a substitute for a program drawing.

A separate Chinese design study gives a smaller 10 kW example: a 20CrMnTi hollow gear shaft with a 27 mm inner diameter, 33–60 mm outer diameter, 80–250 mm length, 28 Nm peak torque, and 12,000 rpm [Zhang et al., 2018](https://publica.fraunhofer.de/bitstreams/a343908c-8dd5-4ed6-bcbf-366b0a2a9d09/download). That case demonstrates that the product family covers more than one size class; it is not a universal NEV specification.

The [FITGEN e-axle report](https://www.fitgen-project.eu/files/FITGEN_D1.3_Reliable%20and%20scalable%20design%20ready%20for%20mass%20manufacturing%20and%20dismantling.pdf) describes a reference rotor operating in the 20,000–22,000 rpm range after exceeding an 18,000 rpm project target. It is useful for high-speed screening, but it does not provide the shaft drawing, wall thickness, balance grade, or shaft-level runout requirements.

### 1.3 Why the hollow section is valuable—and where it becomes dangerous

For a thin-walled circular shaft, the polar second moment is:

\[
J=\frac{\pi}{32}(D_o^4-D_i^4),\quad \tau_{\max}=\frac{16TD_o}{\pi(D_o^4-D_i^4)}
\]

where \(D_o\) is outside diameter, \(D_i\) is inside diameter, \(T\) is torque, and \(\tau_{\max}\) is the nominal maximum torsional shear stress.

For equal outside diameter and length, the mass ratio of a hollow shaft to a solid shaft is approximately:

\[
\frac{m_h}{m_s}=1-\left(\frac{D_i}{D_o}\right)^2
\]

The hollow section removes material near the neutral core, so mass can fall substantially while much of the torsional section modulus remains. However, the stiffness and strength penalties accelerate as the wall becomes thin, particularly under combined torsion and bending.

JEC reports that its 2024–2026 dataset of 22 EV traction-motor shaft programs found 30–40% mass reduction when solid 4140 was replaced by hollow 4140, with no measurable fatigue-life penalty in the tested continuous-duty context when the wall remained above 25% of outside diameter. The same source describes approximately 35% wall as a typical choice, 25% as a lower-margin limit requiring fatigue testing, and 50% as an excessive mass-saving target with a large fatigue penalty [JEC EV shaft requirements](https://www.motor-shaft.com/news/ev-motor-shaft-requirements-high-speed-high-torque-and-lightweight-design-challenges/). Because the source does not define the wall-thickness convention in a way that can be reconciled with every shaft drawing, this threshold must remain a screening rule rather than a general design law.

An illustrative calculation shows the trade-off. If a hypothetical shaft has \(D_o=50\) mm and a 5 mm radial wall, then \(D_i=40\) mm. The material cross-sectional area is 36% lower than that of a solid 50 mm shaft, while the ideal polar stiffness is about 59% of the solid value. This calculation is only geometric; it does not include bearing span, stress concentrations, rotor mass, critical speed, fatigue notch effects, or manufacturing defects.

The hollow section may also be used as a functional passage. Fink describes internal cooling for weight reduction, rotor cooling, and oil transport to the gearbox, with cleanliness requirements for gravimetric contamination and particle size. Gai’s thesis analyzes forced coolant flow through a hollow automotive traction-motor shaft and warns that shaft rotation creates secondary flow, making a stationary-shaft heat-transfer correlation invalid [Gai, 2020](https://theses.ncl.ac.uk/jspui/bitstream/10443/5024/1/Gai%20Y%202020.pdf). The FITGEN reference unit specifies 6–10 l/min of a 50/50 water-glycol mixture around the stator, but that is not evidence of a shaft-integrated cooling passage [FITGEN D1.3](https://www.fitgen-project.eu/files/FITGEN_D1.3_Reliable%20and%20scalable%20design%20ready%20for%20mass%20manufacturing%20and%20dismantling.pdf).

### 1.4 Speed, critical speed, balance, and runout

The shaft must remain dynamically stable over the complete operating range, including acceleration through resonances and high-speed operation above the first critical speed where the design permits supercritical running.

Available speed figures describe different application classes:

| Evidence or application class | Reported speed range or criterion | Interpretation |
|---|---:|---|
| JEC field dataset | 12,000–20,000 rpm continuous; 18,000–24,000 rpm typical first critical speed | Supplier-reported production-program range |
| FITGEN reference e-axle | 20,000–22,000 rpm rotor speed | High-speed project reference |
| Fink industrial experience | 20,000–30,000 rpm maximum speed | High-speed rotor-shaft envelope |
| Zhang et al. | Critical speed 20–25% above operating speed | Design rule in one electric-motor case |
| IMARC e-axle facility | 18,000 rpm dynamometer capability | Facility test envelope, not shaft specification |

The differences are not necessarily contradictory. Critical speed depends on shaft diameter and length, bearing span, rotor mass distribution, housing stiffness, and the location of gears, laminations, and balancing disks. The [JEC field guide](https://www.motor-shaft.com/news/ev-motor-shaft-requirements-high-speed-high-torque-and-lightweight-design-challenges/) emphasizes that the first bending frequency is a shaft-and-bearing-system property, not solely a material-strength property.

Balance grade must also be assigned to the complete rotor system and test speed. JEC reports G2.5 at rated speed and possible G1.0 requirements for permanent-magnet motors above 15,000 rpm. General industrial guidance maps G6.3 to ordinary electric motors and G2.5 to medium and large motors, while noting that tighter grades require more balancing runs [Lütgert balancing guidance](https://www.luetgert-antriebe.de/luetgert-neu-en/competences/mechanical-processing/balancing-according-to-din-iso-21940.php). These are application recommendations, not one universal hollow-shaft grade.

ISO 1940-1:2003 specified residual-unbalance tolerances and verification methods for rigid rotors, but that edition is withdrawn and was revised by ISO 21940-11:2016. ISO 21940-21:2022 addresses acceptance testing of balancing machines and emphasizes rotor-specific calibration at a defined mass and speed [ISO 1940-1](https://www.iso.org/standard/27092.html); [ANSI summary of ISO 21940-21:2022](https://blog.ansi.org/ansi/iso-21940-21-mechanical-vibration-rotor-balancing/). A production drawing should therefore specify the applicable current standard, residual unbalance, correction planes, balancing speed, and whether the requirement applies to the shaft, rotor subassembly, or complete motor.

### 1.5 Material and volume assumptions

Official and industrial NEV shaft specifications support a steel-centered assessment. T/ZJDJ 002-2022 preferentially lists 20CrMnTi, 20CrNiMo, 40Cr, and 42CrMo, together with the corresponding “H” grades under Chinese standards [T/ZJDJ 002-2022](https://ndls.cnis.ac.cn/standard/detail/1bf70fee23d908c4df27c754520158da). The 2026 T/CMEEEA 069 listing explicitly covers both solid and hollow motor shafts in pure-electric and plug-in-hybrid drive-motor systems [T/CMEEEA 069-2026](https://ndls.cnis.ac.cn/standard/detail/d5869705e3643a28e922abd0e5e14660). T/CAAMTB 265-2025 addresses hollow split-structure shafts press-fitted at room temperature, showing that split hollow architectures are now recognized in an NEV-specific manufacturing specification [T/CAAMTB 265-2025](https://ndls.cnis.ac.cn/standard/detail/e69a321a53a870b0b33c0d0ad403f82b).

There is no validated target-program specification combining shaft dimensions, torque spectrum, critical speed, wall thickness, balance, runout, fluid passage, heat-treatment distortion, and annual shaft volume. E-axle capacity should not be confused with shaft capacity: one facility case reports 240,000 integrated e-axles per year, expandable to 360,000, but does not state the number of hollow shafts produced [IMARC e-axle facility](https://www.imarcengineering.com/case-study/electric-motor-and-e-axle-manufacturing-facility).

Accordingly, the economic comparison below uses three qualitative volume situations:

- prototype or low volume: tooling amortization is weak and flexibility dominates;
- serial production: dedicated forming and automated machining begin to offset tooling;
- high volume: repeatability, cycle time, yield, automation, and amortized tooling dominate.

The supplied evidence does not support numerical unit costs or universal break-even quantities for a named NEV shaft. The FIA forging guide gives broad process indicators—impression-die forging is associated with 300 or more pieces typically, cold forging with usually more than 10,000, open-die forging with one or more and up to about 50 typical, and rolled rings with 10 or more typical—but these are general forging ranges, not shaft-specific break-even points [Forging Industry Association guide](https://www.forging.org/Common/Uploaded%20files/Design%20Engineering%20Center/Product%20Design%20Guide%20for%20Forging.pdf).

## 2. Current forming-technology landscape

### 2.1 Process inventory and maturity

The following inventory covers the forming families that can produce a hollow shaft, a hollow near-net preform, or a shaft-integrated feature. A complete production route normally combines more than one family.

| Named technique | Hollow output or preform | Maturity for NEV shafts | Suitable scale | Main limitation |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Open-die and mandrel forging | Large hollow shell, tube, stepped bore, or prototype preform | Established forging technology; niche for small NEV shafts | Prototype, low volume, large or unusual geometry | Low precision and substantial machining |
| Hot, warm, or cold impression-die forging | Solid or hollow near-net shaft, flanges, end forms, splines | Established automotive forming family; direct EV evidence is industrial but not fully quantified | Medium to very high volume | High tooling and force; bore and undercuts may need secondary work |
| Flashless, net-shape, and near-net forging | Close-to-final external features and selected holes or splines | Established in selected automotive components; shaft-specific qualification required | High volume | Tight billet-volume control and heat-treatment distortion |
| Upsetting, heading, and high-speed end forming | Enlarged ends, flanges, bearing bosses, local features | Established as a feature-forming operation | High volume for repeated end forms | Limited by unsupported length and buckling |
| Forward, backward, impact, and composite extrusion | Hollow cylinders, stepped bores, splines, gear or end features | Industrial for selected shaft features; direct NEV composite-extrusion evidence is mainly simulation | High volume for simple repeatable geometry | High forming loads, tool stress, formability and die life |
| Radial forging with mandrel | Stepped hollow monobloc, bottle-shaped shaft, internal contours | Strong automotive and supplier evidence; direct EV route is conditional | Serial to high volume | Tooling/process control, inner-hole distortion and damage |
| Rotary swaging | Thin-wall or variable-wall tube, external and internal reductions | Industrially relevant and directly promoted for rotor shafts; finished-shaft evidence remains limited | Serial to high volume | Friction, wall-thickness variation, multi-pass burden |
| Axial forming and spline extrusion | Internal splines, helical or axial features on hollow blank | Industrially established feature process | High volume | Requires run-out space or compatible profile |
| Spline rolling and helical-gear forming | External spline or helical feature on tube or shaft | Industrially evidenced | High volume | Runout, pitch error, tube deformation and tool loading |
| Cross-wedge or skew rolling | Stepped hollow preform or shaft section | Automotive rolling technology; hollow motor-shaft evidence is mainly simulation or analogue | Medium to high volume if qualified | Cavities, surface hollows, tool wear and machining allowance |
| Rotary compression or rotary forging | Stepped hollow shaft over mandrel | Laboratory demonstrated | Prototype to conditional serial | Limited production evidence and complex load control |
| Ring rolling | Seamless ring or annular flange preform | Established for rings; not normally a complete elongated motor shaft | Low to high volume for ring features | Does not directly create a complete rotor shaft |
| Seamless tube piercing, mandrel rolling, drawing, and sinking | Seamless hollow tube with controlled wall and bore | Established tube technology; direct motor-shaft qualification limited | Serial to high volume | Inner-surface defects, drawing/annealing and grinding burden |
| Flow forming, tube spinning, and rotary drawing | Tapered or stepped thin-wall tube | Technically established in other sectors; conditional for NEV shafts | Prototype to serial | Material and thermal control, multiple passes |
| Tube hydroforming and warm/hot gas forming | Stepped or contoured tube preform | Established in automotive structures; emerging for motor shafts | High volume only if geometry and capital justify it | High pressure, tooling, control complexity and cycle time |
| Friction-welded split or hybrid shaft | Nested tubes, forged ends, or separate flanges | Industrially plausible; NEV-specific standards cover split structures | Serial to high volume | Weld fatigue, runout, balance, inspection and assembly |
| Powder forging | Dense near-net symmetric component | Mature for selected automotive parts; weak hollow-shaft evidence | High volume | Hollow geometry, porosity control and limited shaft evidence |
| Additive manufacture | Direct hollow lattice or complex shaft | Emerging material capability but unqualified for production NEV shafts | Prototype or special low volume | Build rate, anisotropy, fatigue, balance, cost and post-processing |
| Machining from bar or tube | Finished shaft without bulk forming | Established fallback and prototype route | Prototype, low volume, changing variants | High chip volume, material waste, long cycle time |

This taxonomy reflects the distinction between a process that can shape the complete shaft and one that only creates a local feature. For example, Kinefac describes spline extrusion as a high-rate net-shape operation on a solid or hollow blank, but Fink’s production route still turns and drills the shaft before heat treatment. “Net shape” therefore applies to a profile or operation, not automatically to the whole motor shaft.

### 2.2 Historical transition in shaft manufacture

The principal transition has been from solid bar machining or welded assemblies toward near-net bulk forming, hollow tube forming, and integrated feature forming.

Machining from bar remains geometrically flexible, but the FIA guide notes that much of the purchased stock is removed as chips and that forged grain flow generally provides better material utilization and fatigue behavior. Fink’s cited internal global study reports that 95% of industrial rotor shafts in its surveyed population begin with a forging, while only 5% begin as bar or tube followed by machining [Hirschvogel rotor-shaft paper](https://www.hirschvogel.com/fileadmin/user_upload/ATZlive_Paper_HIVO_Rotorshaft_klf_V6.pdf). The survey’s sample and market definition are not disclosed, so the figure is an industrial indicator rather than a universal market statistic.

The second transition is from solid forgings to hollow, internally controlled preforms. Mandrels, radial forging, rotary swaging, extrusion, tube drawing, flow forming, and hydroforming are all attempts to place material where torque, bearing, spline, and assembly loads require it while removing material from the low-stress core.

The third transition is integration. Modern routes increasingly combine forming with axial spline forming, helical-gear forming, local hardening, and automated machining. Felss describes a six-station cold-forming chain that combines rotary swaging and axial forming from tube stock, while Profiroll describes NC-controlled rolling of a full-length involute spline on a thin-walled hollow rotor shaft [Felss rotor-shaft process chain](https://felss.com/en/blog/from-cost-factor-to-competitive-advantage-an-efficient-process-chain-for-rotor-shafts/); [Profiroll hollow rotor shaft](https://www.profiroll.com/fileadmin/user_upload/4_verfahren/5_Bibliothek/eMobility-Rotor_shaft.pdf).
