| Nitro with protein or hydrocolloid | Velvety, creamy, visually dramatic; can make vegetable or tea bases feel substantial | Immediate after batching; small-batch preparation | Listed Kisag hardware totals CHF 277.90 before consumables | Requires trained dispensing, allergen control, and immediate service for best texture |
| Vacuum de-alcoholization | Can retain category flavor from an alcoholic starting liquid but risks aroma loss and oxidation | Process and validation burden are substantial | Highest regulatory and equipment complexity | Residual ABV must be analytically verified; not a routine bar method |

The cost column is deliberately conservative. The supplied evidence contains equipment and ingredient benchmarks but no uniform labor study comparing every method. Rotovap output, nitro hardware, and pairing labor provide anchors; they do not constitute a complete cost model.

### Operational evidence from current programs

High-end pairing programs show that labor can dominate raw-material cost. Geranium’s non-alcoholic pairing is reported at 1,300 Danish kroner, with 30–45 hours per week devoted to drinks work across the pairing program. At Hiša Franko, five kilograms of buckwheat amazake raw material cost €6, but the drink requires three stages beginning with a 24-hour fermentation; time therefore contributes materially to pricing. At Mater Iniciativa, plant material can oxidize or change color and flavor within minutes, requiring constant attention ([SevenFifty Daily pairing-menu report](https://daily.sevenfifty.com/non-alcoholic-pairing-menus/)).

These cases caution against using ingredient cost as a proxy for operational feasibility. A fermented rice drink may be inexpensive in raw materials but expensive in labor. A hydrosol may use water and leaves but require specialized equipment and hours of preparation. A kegged drink may have a higher initial equipment cost but reduce service minutes during a rush.

Backbar Academy’s 2026 operator guidance benchmarks alcoholic cocktails at 18–22% pour cost and suggests 10–15% for N/A cocktails. Its worked Negroni comparison is explicitly an example: an alcoholic build at $3.00 cost and $14.00 price versus a zero-proof build at $1.50 cost and $12.00 price. These are operator benchmarks, not universal observations, and they do not account for every labor, waste, tax, or equipment cost ([Backbar Academy pricing guide](https://academy.getbackbar.com/pricing-non-alcoholic-menu-strategy)).

The practical conclusion is that a non-alcoholic menu should combine service formats. A fast commercial-base highball can protect a busy shift. A clarified or hydrosol drink can serve as a premium signature. A kegged spritz can support events. A nitro or pairing drink can justify labor when the service context supports it.

### What consumers accept, and what they notice

The Mora study suggests that consumer acceptance can remain comparable when the drink retains recognizable balance, temperature, presentation, and social context. It does not imply that consumers cannot detect differences. The NoLo versions generated descriptors such as watery, sweet, cardamom, kombucha, and gas, showing where formulation work remains visible.

The beer studies and product review suggest three recurring sensory risks:

- reduced body and warmth;
- aroma that is either too subdued or too sharply botanical;
- sweetness used as a substitute for structure.

Current successful menus address these risks through tannin, acid, smoke, savory components, body systems, and carbonation rather than simply increasing sugar.

## 6. Safety, Stability, Storage, and Non-Alcoholic Verification

### ABV terminology is jurisdiction-specific

The word “non-alcoholic” does not guarantee one global alcohol threshold. The 2026 TTB presentation describes beverages below 0.5% ABV as non-alcoholic and 0.0% ABV as alcohol-free, while noting that specific definitions apply to malt beverages ([TTB Low-No Alcohol Products, 2026](https://www.ttb.gov/system/files/2026-02/Low-No_Alcohol_Products_for_TTB_web-_FINAL.pdf)).

The current England-and-Wales guidance is stricter and more conditional. Business Companion reports:

- “alcohol-free” at no more than 0.05% ABV, only where alcohol has been extracted;
- “de-alcoholised” at no more than 0.5% ABV, where alcohol has been extracted;
- “low alcohol” at 1.2% ABV or below;
- “non-alcoholic” should not be paired with a name commonly associated with an alcoholic drink.

The UK Department of Health and Social Care consultation discusses possible changes but does not itself establish a new final threshold ([Business Companion guidance updated March 2026](https://www.businesscompanion.info/en/quick-guides/food-and-drink/alcoholic-beverages-and-alcohol-in-food); [DHSC consultation](https://www.gov.uk/government/consultations/updating-labelling-guidance-for-no-and-low-alcohol-alternatives/updating-labelling-guidance-for-no-and-low-alcohol-alternatives-consultation)).

At EU level, the situation is not harmonized. A 2023 analysis reported no EU-wide definition for low/no-alcohol beer or even regular beer, although the Combined Nomenclature includes a code for non-alcoholic beer below 0.5% ABV. Sixteen Member States were reported to have national legislation with varying thresholds ([Food Compliance International](https://foodcomplianceinternational.com/industry-insight/scholarly-articles/3255-low-and-no-alcohol-beer-in-the-eu-status-and-legal-challenges)).

Spain illustrates the problem. MenuSmart reports that the Spanish beer category *cerveza sin alcohol* is below 1% ABV and therefore does not mean 0.0%. The threshold applies to Spanish beer, not automatically to cocktails or all beverages ([MenuSmart’s 13 September 2026 guide](https://www.menusmart.dev/blogs/non-alcoholic-drinks-menu-guide)). A 2022 comparative review lists Germany below 0.5%, Spain at 1%, France at 1.2%, and the United Kingdom at 0.05% for alcohol-free products ([Okaru and Lachenmeier review](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9506306/)).

The supplied evidence does not include current official guidance for Singapore, India, or the United Arab Emirates. A comparative table lists India at 0.5% or below, but that is not a substitute for a current national regulatory determination. Singapore, India, and UAE ABV-labeling fields should therefore be treated as unavailable until checked against the applicable authority and product category.

### Stated, residual, and verified ABV

Three different statements must be kept separate:

1. a venue or producer calls a drink zero-proof or 0.0%;
2. a packaged ingredient has a declared residual range;
3. a laboratory assay verifies the finished mixed drink or batch.

Mont Bar’s release calls its pairing 0.0%, and Atelier V calls its menu 0% ABV. These are stated program claims; no independent measurements are supplied. Top Hat calls the Pathfinder Mule fully zero-proof, but again provides no analytical result. Seedlip’s FAQ permits trace alcohol below 0.5% undiluted even though product listings may present the range as 0.0%. Three Spirit Livener may permit up to 0.5% alcohol according to the 2026 product review.

A complete drink can also acquire alcohol from less obvious components. Bitters, flavor extracts, tinctures, fermented mixers, kombucha, kefir, and spirit-derived ingredients may contain alcohol even when the principal base does not. MenuSmart specifically warns that removing the main spirit is insufficient if alcoholic bitters or flavorings remain in the recipe.

Fermentation is not proof of alcohol-free status. The 2026 traditional-fermentation review reports that kefir is usually below 2% alcohol and below 0.3% for Turkish kefir. The NoLo review reports that Brazilian kombucha can be below 0.5% or above 0.5% depending on production, and that boza ranges from low alcohol in Turkey to substantially higher levels in Egypt. FlavorSum reports a 6.8% ABV tepache product and notes that some tepache producers raise the alcohol level to 5% or more ([FlavorSum fermented beverage examples](https://flavorsum.com/innovation-non-alcoholic-fermented-beverages/)).

For a drink intended for abstainers, religious requirements, pregnancy, medication restrictions, or regulatory claims, ABV verification needs to cover the actual finished batch and the complete ingredient chain.

### pH and water activity

pH and water activity address different risks. The FDA defines water activity as the ratio of a food’s vapor pressure to that of distilled water under the same conditions. Most foods have water activity above 0.95, which can support bacterial, yeast, and mold growth. The FDA states that a finished product at water activity 0.85 or below falls outside specified U.S. regulations for certain low-acid canned and acidified foods, but this threshold is not a universal guarantee of shelf stability ([FDA water-activity guidance](https://www.fda.gov/inspections-compliance-enforcement-and-criminal-investigations/inspection-technical-guides/water-activity-aw-foods)).

The FDA also warns that temperature control is important during measurement: at 25°C, a 0.1°C difference between sample and surrounding air can shift the reading by approximately 0.005 aw. Water activity rises with temperature, so a value measured under one storage condition cannot automatically be applied to another.

Icon Foods recommends designing acidified non-alcoholic RTDs to equilibrium pH no higher than 4.6, with a practical formulation range of approximately pH 3.0–3.6, and recommends working with a process authority. Its margarita benchmark targets pH 3.2–3.4. These are useful development targets, not evidence that every cocktail with citrus is safe at room temperature.

The fermented-cereal review associates pH 2.5–3.5 with improved safety and shelf life but emphasizes that pH must be considered together with water activity. A low pH does not control every organism, nor does it address spoilage yeasts, packaging contamination, or continued fermentation.

No recipe-specific pH or water-activity values are supplied for Garden View, the Pathfinder Mule, the Mont Bar pairing, the Native drinks, the Connaught drinks, the Nitro Carrot Gingertini, or the Smoked Bloody Mary.

### Preservation and processing

Removing alcohol removes part of the beverage’s natural microbial protection. The NoLo review states that low-strength products containing fermentable carbohydrates are vulnerable to lactic acid bacteria, coliforms, molds, and yeasts. Such products are commonly heat-sterilized or aseptically packaged when sold as packaged beverages, but the review does not assign a shelf life to an individual cocktail.

Available preservation options include:

- acidification with citric, malic, tartaric, or acetic acid;
- pasteurization or validated thermal processing;
- aseptic filling;
- potassium sorbate or sodium benzoate under applicable regulations;
- DMDC where permitted and properly dosed;
- refrigeration;
- low-bioburden production and hygienic packaging;
- controlled carbonation and cold-chain handling.

Icon Foods warns that benzoates combined with ascorbic acid, heat, and light create a benzene-risk scenario. It identifies sorbate or DMDC as alternatives in appropriate systems and states that DMDC is used immediately before filling in low-bioburden product. These are process-development considerations, not a permission to add preservatives without regulatory and process review.

The Top Hat keg procedures are operational controls rather than preservation validation. Refrigerating for eight or twelve hours before first service improves carbonation. Daily pressure checks support quality. Neither instruction establishes a safe multi-day shelf life for the batch.

### Storage and shelf-life evidence

| Component or drink | Supplied storage or shelf-life statement | What remains unknown |
|---|---|---|
| Seedlip Spice 94, Garden 108, Grove 42 | Two-year unopened best-before; consume within six months after opening; cool, shaded storage; refrigeration not required according to FAQ | Product-specific pH, water activity, microbial validation, and independent ABV |
| Garden View shichimi-lemon syrup | Refrigerate after cooling | Shelf life, pH, preservative system, and aw |
| Fermented rhubarb shrub | Two to three months refrigerated; flavor often best at one to two weeks | Validation method, batch variability, and post-opening handling |
| Vinegar shrub | Drink Balo reports six months refrigerated | No challenge study or universal applicability |
| Clarified milk punch | Refrigerate after two filtration passes | No duration, microbial validation, pH, or aw |
| Pathfinder Mule | Refrigerated four to eight hours before first service; daily carbonation checks | No packaged shelf life or microbial stability |
| Ginger Yuzu Tonic | Refrigerate 12–24 hours before first service; carbonation procedure includes repeated checks | No shelf life after carbonation |
| Kombucha and fermented fruit drinks | Refrigeration and controlled fermentation are implied or recommended in supplied examples | Product-specific alcohol drift, microbial stability, and shelf life |
| Fresh juice, egg-white, and nitro drinks | Immediate service is the practical format in the supplied recipes | No validated hold time, pathogen control, or packaged stability |

The correct conclusion is not that these drinks are unstable. It is that the supplied evidence does not establish comparable shelf lives. A two-month fermented shrub claim, a six-month vinegar-shrub claim, and a refrigerated clarification instruction measure different things and should not be ranked as equivalent.

### Allergens and functional ingredients

The most visible allergen risks are dairy in clarified milk punch, egg white in Nitro Carrot Gingertini, and potentially soy, gluten-containing grains, or other allergens in miso, shoyu, freekeh, barley tea, bread kvass, or botanical products. The catalog records do not provide complete allergen declarations for every menu example.

Seedlip’s FAQ warns that people with quinine hypersensitivity or relevant pre-existing conditions should consult a doctor. Livener contains guayusa and green tea and is reported to provide almost 60 mg caffeine per 1.7 oz serving. Serious Eats also notes that adaptogens are not well supported by high-quality human data and may create concerns for people with gastrointestinal, diabetes, blood-pressure, autoimmune, pregnancy, or breastfeeding conditions.

Functional ingredients should therefore be treated as formulation and labeling variables, not as automatic health benefits. A menu can offer botanical complexity without making unsupported wellness claims.

## 7. Transferable Innovations and Formulation Opportunities

### Evidence grades

The following grades distinguish what is already demonstrated from what is promising but still requires development:

- **Direct current zero-proof example:** a named recent drink or program explicitly described as non-alcoholic, 0.0%, or zero-proof.
- **Current venue or producer report:** a contemporary program with qualitative formulation information but incomplete quantities.
- **Published recipe:** a named recipe with quantities and method, but date or continuing availability may be unavailable.
- **Product specification:** manufacturer or product-review information, usually useful for ingredients and serving but not for finished cocktail performance.
- **Scholarly transfer evidence:** controlled sensory, fermentation, or food-safety evidence from beer, wine, tea, or other matrices.
- **General development guidance:** a formulation or industry recommendation without independent validation.

### High-value formulation patterns

| Design pattern | Compatible methods | Formulation logic | Target effect | Evidence strength and limitation |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Fermented acid plus natural carbonation plus salinity | Lacto-fermented vegetable or fruit, water kefir, seaweed or celery infusion | Let fermentation supply acid and complexity; use salt or umami to prevent a sweet-soda profile | Savory, food-compatible, lively finish | Direct current evidence from Mont Bar; no published ratios, pH, or ABV verification |
| Hydrosol plus cordial plus force carbonation | Water-based rotovap hydrosol, citrus cordial, chilled water, keg carbonation | Isolate a seasonal aroma, add controlled acid and sugar, then use gas for lift | Precise aroma and highball drinkability | Direct zero-proof Kitchen Table example; equipment and batch parameters unavailable |
| Tea or tannin plus acid, smoke, and controlled spice | Cold-brewed lapsang, black tea, jasmine, citrus, smoke, ginger or chili | Use tannin for grip, smoke for category identity, and spice for calibrated warmth | Replaces parts of ethanol’s finish without excessive sweetness | Direct recipe evidence for Smoked Bloody Mary and venue evidence from Sexy Fish; dose and sensory head-to-head data limited |
| Clarification plus hydrocolloid body | Tea, acid, milk or yogurt, filtration, xanthan | Remove harsh tannin and haze, then restore viscosity without losing clarity | Clear, soft, rounded, premium mouthfeel | Detailed published zero-proof recipe; shelf-life and dosage validation incomplete |
| Shrub or kombucha plus citrus and controlled carbonation | Vinegar or fermented shrub, kombucha, fresh juice, keg or sparkling water | Combine known acid with fermentation aromatics and final gas | Bright, complex, low-spirit highball | Multiple current recipes and producer guides; alcohol drift and stability require control |
| Botanical base plus custom syrup and bitter finish | Seedlip, Everleaf, Ghia, Three Spirit, coriander or spice syrup, gentian or tea | Use the commercial base for speed; build local identity in the modifier | Fast service with a more complete mid-palate | Many current examples; some product reviews find bases underwhelming without support |
| Vegetable or fruit purée plus protein or nitro | Carrot, tomato, coconut, aquafaba or egg white, nitro | Replace lost weight and create a visual service moment | Velvety body and immediate sensory impact | Nitro Carrot Gingertini is a direct recipe; allergen, hold-time, and equipment constraints remain |
| Fat-washed fermented or fruit base | Cocoa butter, fruit juice, tea, fermentation | Add aromatic richness and coating texture to a low-alcohol or zero-proof base | Deeper, more gastronomic finish | Direct Mont Bar example; no published parameters or repeatability data |
| Controlled de-alcoholization plus hydrosol restoration | Alcoholic starting liquid, vacuum process, botanical hydrosol | Preserve familiar category flavor while replacing lost volume and aroma | Spirit-like profile | Current bar reports and patent evidence; residual ABV, licensing, yield, and stability are unresolved |

### Why the first five combinations are especially promising

#### Fermentation plus natural carbonation

This is the most distinctive current culinary pattern because it generates acidity and fizz through the same biological system. Mont Bar demonstrates the combination with tomato, celery, seaweed, and water kefir. A development team could use the pattern with fruit, vegetable, tea, or cereal bases, but the variables must be controlled: substrate sugar, inoculum, fermentation endpoint, temperature, cold storage, and ABV.

The limitation is not sensory potential but verification. A drink that continues fermenting after packaging can become more acidic, more carbonated, and more alcoholic. The U.S. TTB warning, as summarized by MenuSmart, specifically identifies post-bottling kombucha fermentation as an alcohol-content risk.

#### Hydrosol plus cordial plus force carbonation

This is a high-value pairing-menu pattern. The hydrosol can express an ingredient such as oyster leaf, cucumber, rose, or herb without the heaviness of a syrup or purée. A cordial supplies acid and sugar, and force carbonation provides service lift.

Its limitation is access and throughput. The Kimball House benchmark of four hours for 2 liters illustrates why a rotovap drink may be a special or premium pairing rather than a high-volume menu staple. Water-based hydrosols also need protection from oxidation and should be evaluated for storage rather than assumed to be stable.

#### Tea, tannin, smoke, and spice

This is the most accessible sensory replacement system. A bar can cold-brew tea with standard equipment, combine it with acid and sweetener, and add smoke or spice in low doses. The Smoked Bloody Mary is a clear example: lapsang replaces the vodka volume and contributes tannin and smoke that align with the tomato.

The limitation is balance. Tannin, smoke, acid, and chili all dry or intensify the finish. Without enough body or sweetness, the drink becomes austere. With too much, it becomes hot, bitter, or medicinal.

#### Clarification plus hydrocolloid body

Clarification solves a common problem in tea- and citrus-heavy non-alcoholic cocktails: rough tannin, haze, and sediment. Xanthan or another suitable hydrocolloid can restore gloss and viscosity. The technique is particularly useful where a menu wants the visual precision of a clear drink without the thinness associated with clarified liquids.

The limitation is process complexity and allergen management. Milk clarification requires dairy, careful filtration, refrigeration, and a validated storage protocol. Vegan agar clarification is possible, but the supplied non-alcoholic performance evidence is less complete.

#### Shrub or kombucha plus controlled carbonation

This is the most operationally accessible combination for bars that lack a rotovap. Shrubs offer measured acid, fruit depth, and a stable concentrate; kombucha supplies fermentation character and natural acidity. A keg or final sparkling water addition turns either into a service-ready highball.

The limitation is that fermentation is not automatically alcohol-free. Vinegar shrubs offer greater control, while live kombucha offers greater biological variability. A bar should choose between them according to its ABV, shelf-life, and service requirements rather than treating them as interchangeable.

### Regional formulation opportunities

India’s reported zero-proof programs provide a strong model for flavor systems built from local ingredients rather than global spirit analogues. Guava, celery, chili-coriander salt, jalapeño brine, fermented hot honey, black lime air, and specialty sodas can create recognizable structure with regional identity.

Singapore’s Native suggests a second model: use hydrosols, edible oils, local herbs, fruit waste, miso, shoyu, and house ferments to create a non-alcoholic menu that is not dependent on refined sugar. The two-month pineapple shoyu points toward fermentation as a savory flavor-development tool rather than a beverage base alone.

Barcelona’s Mont Bar demonstrates a tasting-menu model in which one produce item is transformed through several methods. This is especially transferable to culinary R&D because it turns the ingredient itself into the organizing principle: fruit fermentation for acid, tea infusion for roasted or cereal notes, fat-washing for coating, and carbonation for service.

London’s Kitchen Table and Connaught show two complementary approaches. Kitchen Table uses specialized extraction to isolate a seasonal aroma for food pairing. Connaught uses more accessible fermented and infused ingredients while preserving familiar high-end service theater.

New York’s Seed Library shows how to adapt signature cocktails without preserving the original spirit logic. A coriander seed Gimlet can be rebuilt around botanical aroma and syrup. A Freekeh French Martini can use grain, fruit, and miso to create a new structural identity rather than attempting to reproduce vodka.

Copenhagen and the broader European pairing tradition demonstrate that non-alcoholic drinks can be designed around food, territory, and season. Peru’s Mater Iniciativa adds another regional model: local and indigenous ingredients, such as cushuro and kunuka from high-altitude ecosystems, can provide concentrated flavor and a sense of place when developed collaboratively and responsibly.

### Practical opportunities by service context

For a high-volume cocktail bar, the strongest opportunities are commercial botanical bases with custom syrups, tea concentrates, shrubs, and kegged carbonation. The design priority is repeatability and short service time.

For a tasting-menu restaurant, hydrosols, clarified punches, fermented vegetables, fat-washing, and ingredient-by-ingredient transformations justify higher labor because the drink is part of the culinary narrative. The priority is pairing accuracy, seasonal identity, and controlled small-batch production.

For events and hotels, kegged Pathfinder-style mules, Ginger Yuzu Tonic, shrub highballs, and packaged products provide predictable service. The priority is batch yield, refrigeration, pressure management, and a fallback format for staffing constraints.

For packaged RTDs, the Icon Foods benchmark illustrates the need to formulate pH, Brix, carbonation, sweetness curve, mouthfeel, preservation, and capsaicin together. A packaged drink needs more than a successful bar recipe: it needs process authority review, ingredient specifications, packaging compatibility, shelf-life testing, and analytical ABV verification.

## Closing judgment

Current non-alcoholic cocktail craft is best understood as structural beverage design. The category has moved from juice, soda, and spirit removal toward a broader toolkit of fermentation, tea, shrubs, clarification, hydrosols, culinary umami, controlled spice, body systems, carbonation, and nitro service.

The most robust transferable principle is modularity. Build aroma separately from body, acid separately from sweetness, bitterness separately from warmth, and carbonation separately from preservation. Then verify the complete drink rather than assuming that a non-alcoholic base makes the finished cocktail 0.0%.

Fermentation and hydrosols offer the greatest creative differentiation, while tea, shrubs, clarification, and kegging offer the clearest balance between innovation and operational feasibility. The best current programs combine these methods selectively: a fermented or botanical base for identity, tea or bittering for structure, acid and salt for balance, a body system for weight, and controlled gas or garnish for finish. Their limitations—residual alcohol, microbial change, allergens, equipment burden, and incomplete shelf-life evidence—are not peripheral details. They are part of the formulation.

article:
# Light-Based Therapies in Aesthetic Medicine: Evidence for Photoaging, Brightening, and Hyperpigmentation Through 2026

Current evidence supports laser and IPL treatment for selected forms of photoaging and focal pigmentation, but their roles are indication-specific rather than interchangeable. Pigment-selective lasers generally provide the most direct and rapid treatment for discrete solar lentigines, while fractional lasers and IPL can address broader combinations of pigmentation, erythema, texture, and wrinkles. Melasma may improve with carefully selected laser or combination protocols, but relapse is common and treatment should remain adjunctive to rigorous photoprotection and, usually, topical or systemic therapy. LED and photobiomodulation have credible but generally modest evidence for photoaging; they are not established treatments for melasma or generalized hyperpigmentation. No supplied clinical evidence supports generalized facial “skin whitening.”

The clinically defensible terminology is targeted tone evening, reduction of visible dyschromia, restoration toward the patient’s natural color, or clearance of a defined lesion. The American Academy of Dermatology describes the goals of melasma treatment as reducing pigment production and evening skin tone back to the patient’s natural color, not changing overall constitutional skin color ([AAD melasma guidance](https://www.aad.org/public/diseases/a-z/melasma-treatment)).

This review first defines the relevant conditions and evidence standards. It then catalogs laser, IPL, and LED applications, examines recent technological advances from 2020 through 2026, separates solar lentigines from melasma, and compares the modalities on efficacy, speed, durability, downtime, phototype suitability, and safety. The final sections address combination protocols, personalization, adverse effects, regulatory and ethical limits, and the gaps that prevent a universal treatment ranking.

## Scope, terminology, and evidence context

### What the treatments are intended to change

“Photoaging” refers to visible and structural changes caused largely by cumulative ultraviolet and visible-light exposure. Clinically relevant endpoints include fine and coarse wrinkles, roughness, enlarged pores, laxity, mottled pigmentation, erythema, and loss of dermal density or elasticity. A treatment that improves a wrinkle index or texture score has demonstrated improvement in that measured feature; it has not necessarily restored all components of photodamaged skin.

“Solar lentigines,” often called age spots or sun spots, are discrete, usually well-demarcated epidermal macules on chronically sun-exposed skin. They are fundamentally different from melasma. Their pigment is usually more superficial and localized, making selective pigment targeting especially relevant. Nevertheless, a clinically brown macule can resemble pigmented actinic keratosis, seborrheic keratosis, lichen planus-like keratosis, or lentigo maligna. Cosmetic treatment should follow diagnostic assessment rather than replace it. The 2026 report on a 532-nm green laser excluded equivocal lesions and considered biopsy when dermoscopy could not establish a benign diagnosis ([Zappia et al., 2026, 532-nm green laser case series and review](https://www.mdpi.com/2079-9284/13/3/128)).

“Melasma” is a chronic, relapsing disorder characterized by facial patches of excess pigmentation, commonly involving the forehead, cheeks, nose, and upper lip. Its biology includes melanocyte hyperactivity, epidermal and dermal melanin, pigmentary incontinence, basement-membrane disruption, vascular changes, inflammation, hormonal influences, oxidative stress, and photoaging. The disease is especially common in Fitzpatrick phototypes III–VI and is not simply a superficial deposit that can be permanently removed in one session. A recent review emphasizes that relapse, heterogeneous disease subtypes, post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation (PIH), and inconsistent adherence limit durability ([Targeting Melasma review, 2026](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12783984/)).

“Post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation” (PIH) is pigmentation that follows inflammation or injury, including acne, dermatitis, burns, or energy-based treatment. It is both a treatment target and a major treatment complication. A laser that reduces pre-existing PIH but causes new PIH may provide little net benefit, especially in darker phototypes.

“Brightening” is a useful clinical term only when it is tied to a defined endpoint. It may mean reduced lesion contrast, more even chromametric measurements, reduced melanin index, less erythema, or natural-color restoration. It should not be used to imply generalized bleaching of healthy skin.

| Clinical term | Common objective endpoints | What the endpoint does not prove |
|---|---|---|
| Photoaging | Wrinkle volume or count, roughness, pore area, elasticity, dermal density, VISIA indices, histologic collagen or elastin changes | Complete reversal of intrinsic or extrinsic aging |
| Solar lentigines | Lesion clearance, colorimetry, CIELAB L* change, blinded improvement score, dermoscopic disappearance | Permanent prevention of new lesions or recurrence |
| Melasma | MASI or modified MASI, melanin index, chromametry, VISIA pigment index, physician or patient global assessment | Permanent remission, absence of relapse, or superiority across all phototypes |
| PIH | Change in lesion area, color or melanin index, blinded photographic scoring | Safety against future treatment-induced pigmentation |
| Brightening | Tone homogeneity, reduced mottled pigmentation, restored natural color, reduced erythema | Generalized skin whitening or a change in baseline constitutional skin color |

### Modality definitions

Lasers emit relatively narrow, coherent wavelengths and permit control over pulse duration, fluence, spot size, fractional density, and treatment geometry. Depending on the wavelength and pulse, they may act through selective photothermolysis, photomechanical pigment fragmentation, laser-induced optical breakdown, or controlled thermal remodeling.

IPL is not a laser. It emits a broad, noncoherent spectrum, usually approximately 500–1200 nm, from which cutoff filters select a clinically useful range. Melanin, oxyhemoglobin, and water-related tissue effects can therefore be addressed in one treatment, but the same breadth makes parameter selection and phototype adjustment particularly important.

LED photobiomodulation (PBM) uses low-irradiance visible or near-infrared light without intentional tissue ablation or substantial thermal injury. Red and near-infrared wavelengths are primarily used for cellular and regenerative effects. The clinical dose depends on wavelength, irradiance, fluence, exposure time, distance, device geometry, and repetition. These variables are incompletely standardized.

### Evidence context and skin phototype

The strongest evidence is not evenly distributed across indications. Direct randomized comparisons exist for some laser pairs and for selected combination protocols, but no standardized head-to-head trial comparing laser, IPL, and LED for the same indication, using the same population, treatment schedule, objective endpoint, and follow-up, was retrieved. Relative rankings across modalities must therefore be treated as cross-study impressions rather than definitive comparative efficacy.

The evidence is also concentrated in Fitzpatrick III–V, particularly East Asian cohorts. The 2026 review of 1550- and 1927-nm nonablative fractional lasers included 15 studies, but approximately 79% of the 360 participants were Asian and classified as Fitzpatrick III–IV; only 29 participants were Fitzpatrick V and 9 were Fitzpatrick VI. The review concluded that the dual system is clinically established mainly for Fitzpatrick III–IV and that evidence for Fitzpatrick VI and for 1927-nm treatment remains limited ([1550/1927-nm review in skin of color](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12997386/)).

Phototype is not merely a demographic descriptor. Melanin absorbs much of the 250–1200-nm range, and darker epidermis can compete with the intended target chromophore. Greater melanocyte reactivity also increases the risk that inflammation will produce PIH. A retrospective analysis of 961 sessions of a 1550-nm erbium laser in 422 individuals reported PIH rates of 0.26% for Fitzpatrick II, 2.6% for III, 11.6% for IV, and 33% for V. These values are not universal device risks, but they illustrate why fluence, density, overlap, cooling, and aftercare cannot be separated from the modality itself ([1550/1927-nm review](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12997386/)).

For all three modalities, treatment should be interpreted against photoprotection. The melasma trials that reported sustained improvement generally required frequent broad-spectrum sunscreen use and behavioral sun avoidance. A 2026 review of photoprotection summarized evidence that tinted, iron-oxide-containing sunscreen can reduce melasma relapse more effectively than a colorless formula, although protection against short-wavelength visible light remains formulation-dependent and incomplete ([Azevedo, Lorigo, and Cairrao, 2026](https://doi.org/10.3390/cimb48090921)).

## Laser therapies: current applications and recent advances

### How laser effects are produced

Selective photothermolysis uses wavelength and pulse duration to concentrate energy in a target chromophore while limiting collateral injury. In superficial pigmentation, 532 nm is strongly absorbed by melanin and can fragment or thermally damage melanin-containing structures. Picosecond pulses concentrate energy into a shorter interval and favor photomechanical effects, including pigment fragmentation and, with microlens arrays, laser-induced optical breakdown. Nanosecond Q-switched pulses also target pigment selectively but produce more thermal interaction than picosecond pulses.

Longer wavelengths such as 1064 nm penetrate more deeply and are less strongly absorbed by epidermal melanin than 532 or 755 nm. This can be useful for dermal or mixed pigmentation, but low-fluence “laser toning” requires repeated treatments and can produce mottled hypopigmentation or rebound pigmentation if parameters are excessive or poorly controlled.

Nonablative fractional lasers create microscopic treatment zones while leaving intervening skin intact. A 1550-nm erbium glass laser and a 1927-nm thulium laser primarily target water rather than melanin. The 1550-nm wavelength reaches deeper dermal tissue and is used for remodeling, scars, and some dyschromia; 1927 nm is more strongly absorbed by water and acts more superficially, making it useful for epidermal and superficial dermal pigmentation and photoaging.

Ablative fractional CO2 or Er:YAG lasers remove or vaporize columns of tissue. They can deliver stronger remodeling and facilitate topical delivery, but produce more epidermal injury, inflammation, downtime, and pigmentary risk than nonablative fractional systems.

### Laser modality catalog

| Laser subtype and wavelength | Energy approach and mechanism | Main targets and clinical goals | Typical evidence, protocol, and durability | Safety and evidence maturity |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 532-nm Q-switched or picosecond Nd:YAG/KTP | Melanin-selective photothermal or photomechanical pigment fragmentation | Solar lentigines, freckles, selected superficial PIH; lesion clearance and tone evening | Often one session for lentigines; a 20-person split-face trial used 450-ps 532-nm picosecond versus 10-ns Q-switched treatment and followed patients for 12 weeks | Effective for focal pigment; PIH risk is higher with aggressive endpoints and darker skin. Evidence is strongest for short-term lesion improvement, not recurrence prevention |
| 730-nm picosecond titanium-sapphire | Ultrashort photomechanical pigment fragmentation; proposed greater melanin-to-vascular selectivity | Mixed facial pigmentation, melasma, solar lentigines, PIH | A retrospective 131-person mixed-indication study used 3–6 sessions at 4-week intervals, but wavelength and pulse duration were confounded | Promising emerging option; study reported conflicting parameter ranges and short or incompletely characterized follow-up |
| 755-nm picosecond alexandrite | Photomechanical targeting of melanin, often with flat or diffractive optics | Melasma, lentigines, dermal melanocytosis, photoaging texture | In a 59-person melasma trial, three sessions at 4-week intervals produced 25.5% MASI improvement at week 24; comparable to 2% hydroquinone but inferior to 1064-nm picosecond Nd:YAG | Useful selected option, but PIH, dryness, and focal desquamation occur; not uniformly superior to 1064 nm |
| 1064-nm Q-switched, picosecond, or microsecond Nd:YAG | Low-fluence subcellular pigment disruption; picosecond optical breakdown; microsecond thermal vascular and remodeling effects | Melasma, photoaging, dermal or mixed pigmentation, vascular-inflammatory components | Three-session picosecond treatment improved melasma at 24 weeks; dual low-fluence plus microsecond treatment required 5–10 sessions and had 12-month follow-up | Widely used but relapse-prone; parameter and cumulative-treatment effects are central |
| 1550-nm erbium and 1927-nm thulium nonablative fractional lasers | Water-targeted microscopic thermal zones, epidermal renewal, collagen and elastin remodeling, pigment extrusion | Photoaging, mottled pigmentation, melasma, PIH, scars | Reviews report approximately three sessions at monthly intervals in many studies; 1927-nm trials in facial hyperpigmentation reported improvement maintained to 12 weeks | Established clinical platforms, particularly for selected skin-of-color resurfacing, but PIH risk rises with energy and density |
| Fractional CO2 and Er:YAG | Ablative microcolumns, tissue vaporization, dermal remodeling, enhanced topical delivery | Refractory melasma, scars, texture, selected pigmentary disease | A 30-person refractory-melasma split-face trial used six sessions at 2-week intervals with oral tranexamic acid; CO2 outperformed fractional QS Nd:YAG, but the drug was given to all patients | More inflammatory and downtime-intensive; evidence for melasma is confounded by adjunctive medication and short follow-up |

### Pigment-selective lasers for solar lentigines and focal dyschromia

The clearest laser application in the supplied evidence is the treatment of discrete solar lentigines. In a prospective randomized split-face trial, 20 Korean women with Fitzpatrick III–V skin received one 532-nm picosecond treatment on one side and one 532-nm Q-switched Nd:YAG treatment on the other. The picosecond protocol used 450 ps, 0.3–0.5 J/cm², a 3–4-mm spot, and 2 Hz; the Q-switched protocol used 10 ns, 0.6–0.8 J/cm², the same spot range, and 2 Hz. At 12 weeks, blinded quartile improvement scores were 2.95 for picosecond treatment and 1.8 for Q-switched treatment. PIH occurred in 5% of picosecond-treated sides and 30% of Q-switched-treated sides, although the PIH comparison did not reach statistical significance at p=0.057. Both methods were effective; the trial supports a short-term efficacy and tolerability advantage for picosecond delivery, not proof of permanent clearance ([Kim et al., 2021, 532-nm picosecond versus Q-switched laser](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7992642/)).

The study illustrates why “whitening” is a misleading description. The treatment endpoint was slight whitening of individual lentigines, and the measured result was lesion improvement on a quartile scale. It was not generalized lightening of the surrounding face.

A 2026 Italian case series described a longer-pulsed 532-nm green laser in five patients with one solar lentigo each. All five lesions were classified as complete responses at day 21, with a mean satisfaction score of 8.6/10 and erythema resolving within the first day. The protocol used a 1-mm spot, 16–18 J/cm², 16–18 ms, and one pass with minimal overlap. The result is technically useful because it reports a reproducible protocol and dermoscopic triage, but it cannot establish durable clearance: follow-up was only 21 days, with recurrence, delayed PIH, and later adverse events unmeasured ([Zappia et al., 2026](https://www.mdpi.com/2079-9284/13/3/128)).

The same review places the longer-pulsed approach in context. Older comparative evidence suggests that longer-pulse 532-nm platforms can improve lentigines, but no clinical study establishes their superiority over Q-switched or picosecond systems. Device family, pulse width, fluence, overlap, endpoint intensity, phototype, and aftercare all contribute to the outcome. Aggressive immediate whitening can increase PIH without a clear efficacy advantage, supporting conservative endpoints in darker skin.

A 2026 retrospective comparison of 730-nm picosecond treatment with 532-nm Q-switched Nd:YAG included 131 adults with three different diagnoses: melasma, n=42; solar lentigines, n=60; and PIH, n=29. The 730-nm group had a lower mean post-treatment pigmentation score, 2.55±1.11 versus 3.80±1.40, and a higher reported improvement rate, 56%±10% versus 38%±8%. Adjusted odds of the study’s composite success endpoint were 4.85, with a 95% confidence interval of 2.51–9.38. However, this was retrospective, the groups received different wavelengths and pulse durations, and the source reports inconsistent 730-nm pulse and fluence ranges in different sections. It therefore supports 730 nm as promising, not as proof that the wavelength or picosecond pulse alone caused the difference ([730-nm versus 532-nm comparison](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s40001-026-04099-0)).

For PIH and darker skin, low-energy 1927-nm fractional treatment offers a different strategy. A retrospective photographic review of 61 people with Fitzpatrick IV–VI treated with 5 mJ, 140-μm spots, 170-μm depth, and 5% coverage reported a mean improvement of 43.24% assessed by two independent dermatologists, without reported side effects. The endpoint was facial PIH rather than solar-lentigine-specific clearance, and long-term durability was not reported ([Garg et al. review of laser therapies in skin of color](https://doi.org/10.3390/jcm13072116)).

### 1064-nm lasers for melasma, vascular components, and photoaging

Low-fluence 1064-nm Q-switched Nd:YAG treatment, commonly called laser toning, is widely used in Asian aesthetic practice for melasma. It typically uses large spots, low fluence, multiple passes, and repeated sessions. The intended mechanism is subcellular disruption of melanosomes with limited injury to melanocytes, but the margin between useful pigment reduction and melanocyte damage is narrow.

A prospective randomized assessor-blinded Beijing trial compared three sessions of nonfractional 1064-nm picosecond Nd:YAG, three sessions of nonfractional 755-nm picosecond alexandrite, and twice-daily 2% hydroquinone for 12 weeks. Fifty-nine participants were analyzed: 20 in the 1064-nm group, 20 in the 755-nm group, and 19 in the hydroquinone group. Participants were women with Fitzpatrick III–IV skin. At week 24, four months after the final laser session, MASI improvement was 35.9% for 1064 nm, 25.5% for 755 nm, and 24.0% for hydroquinone. The 1064-nm treatment significantly outperformed both comparators, whereas 755 nm and hydroquinone were comparable ([Liang et al., 2023](https://doi.org/10.3389/fmed.2023.1132823)).

The study’s recurrence findings are more clinically important than the short-term ranking. Recurrence occurred in 4 of 59 participants overall: 5.0% in the 1064-nm group, 10.0% in the 755-nm group, and 5.3% in the hydroquinone group. PIH occurred in approximately 5% of each group and resolved spontaneously within one to six months. All participants applied SPF 48, PA+++ sunscreen at 2 mg/cm² every two hours and used sun-avoidance measures. Thus, the six-month maintenance cannot be attributed to the laser alone. The trial excluded pregnancy, lactation, photosensitive disease, active melasma, recent laser or IPL, recent bleaching products, and inability to follow strict sun protection. It represents a selected, closely supervised population rather than all melasma patients.

A newer dual-mode approach combines low-fluence Q-switched 1064 nm with a 250-μs microsecond 1064-nm mode. The proposed rationale is to address melanin, superficial vascular inflammation, erythema, dermal heating, collagen remodeling, and solar elastosis rather than pigment alone. In a prospective evaluator-blinded split-face trial, 28 Chinese patients were enrolled and 21 completed five to ten monthly sessions. Participants included Fitzpatrick III, IV, and V skin.

At three months after treatment, relapse was 4.8% on the combined side versus 23.8% with low-fluence Q-switched treatment alone, p=0.047. That apparent advantage did not persist: relapse was 23.8% versus 28.6% at six months and 52.4% versus 57.1% at 12 months. MASI improved at one and three months but not significantly at six and 12 months. VISIA pigment indices improved bilaterally, with no significant treatment-side advantage, while the combined side had better red-area indices at one and six months. No treatment-related edema, blistering, PIH, hypopigmentation, infection, or scarring was reported. The appropriate interpretation is a possible short-term benefit for vascular-inflammatory components, not a demonstrated long-term anti-relapse treatment ([dual-mode LFQS plus MPW trial](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12241506/)).

### Nonablative fractional 1550- and 1927-nm lasers

The dual 1550/1927-nm platform is one of the most clinically developed recent technologies for resurfacing and dyschromia in skin of color. The 1550-nm erbium glass wavelength creates dermal microscopic treatment zones and stimulates remodeling; 1927-nm thulium is more strongly absorbed by water and is used for superficial pigment, actinic change, and photoaging. The system reviewed in the United States is described as approved for 1550-nm resurfacing and dyschromia including lentigines and melasma, and for 1927-nm treatment of pigmented lesions including age spots, sunspots, and ephelides. Regulatory indications are jurisdiction-specific and do not by themselves establish effectiveness.

Across 15 studies in Fitzpatrick III–VI, the 1550-nm wavelength consistently improved scarring and melasma, while 1927 nm improved melasma and photoaging. Histologic studies reported increased type I and III collagen, elastic fibers, and hyaluronic acid, as well as reduced melanin. However, biopsy samples were often very small, sometimes only two, three, or 12 participants, so histologic remodeling should not be equated with a validated clinical collagen increase in every patient ([1550/1927-nm review](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12997386/)).

The 1550-nm and 1927-nm wavelengths are not risk-free in darker skin. Lower energy and density were associated with fewer PIH events in studies that directly compared settings. The review’s practical conclusion is that lower coverage, individualized microscopic-treatment-zone density, cooling, and more sessions at lower intensity may provide a safer therapeutic window than a single aggressive treatment.

A randomized study of a nonablative fractional 1927-nm diode laser included 40 adults with moderate-to-severe facial hyperpigmentation and Fitzpatrick III–V skin. Four laser treatments were given at two-week intervals, followed by assessments four and 12 weeks after the last treatment. The Mottled Pigmentation Area and Severity Index improved by approximately 50% at both follow-ups. The comparator was daily 2% hydroquinone or moisturizer, not an untreated control; both comparator groups also showed approximately 50% improvement, and hydroquinone produced better investigator-rated GAIS at week 12. The study supports improvement of facial hyperpigmentation and photodamage, not an age-spot-specific clearance rate or generalized whitening ([Vanaman Wilson et al.](https://doi.org/10.1097/dss.0000000000001521)).

The 2025 systematic review of 1927-nm thulium treatment included 17 studies and 448 participants with various dermatologic conditions. Average protocols involved three sessions at monthly intervals and approximately 120 days of follow-up. Improvements in texture, pigmentation, and scars were common, and adverse effects were generally mild and transient. Melasma relapses occurred, treatment parameters varied considerably, and most studies had moderate-to-high risk of bias. The review supports 1927 nm as promising and clinically useful, but not as a standardized anti-melasma solution ([Oliveira Modena et al., 2025](https://rd.springer.com/content/pdf/10.1007/s10103-025-04781-5.pdf)).

A combination report paired BBL HERO with 1927-nm fractional MOXI, conceptually targeting epidermal pigment with broadband light and superficial dermal pigment with the water-absorbed laser. That approach is discussed below because its clinical evidence is preliminary and difficult to interpret independently of the combination.

### Fractional CO2, Er:YAG, and laser-assisted delivery

Ablative fractional lasers create deeper and more inflammatory microthermal zones than nonablative fractional devices. The potential benefits are stronger remodeling and improved penetration of topical agents. The trade-off is more epidermal disruption, crusting, discomfort, PIH, infection risk, and recovery.

In a prospective split-face trial of 30 patients with refractory melasma, one side received fractional CO2 and the other fractional Q-switched 1064-nm Nd:YAG. All participants also received oral tranexamic acid at 250 mg twice daily, and six sessions were delivered two weeks apart. Patient global assessment favored CO2 at weeks 4, 8, and 12, and MASI declined more on the CO2 side. Erythema and discomfort resolved in less than 24 hours in the report, but the study’s short follow-up and common tranexamic-acid treatment prevent isolation of the laser effect. It supports CO2 as a possible option for carefully selected refractory melasma, not as a first-line universal protocol ([fractional CO2 versus Q-switched Nd:YAG with tranexamic acid](https://doi.org/10.3390/cosmetics8020037)).

A fractional laser can also be used to create microchannels for topical tranexamic acid, vitamin C, cysteamine, or hydroquinone. The rationale is plausible, but the evidence varies by agent, wavelength, dosing, and comparator. Exosome-augmented fractional CO2 treatment is mentioned in recent reviews and small reports, but it remains emerging and lacks large independent comparative trials.

A single case communication illustrates the potential seriousness of pigmentary complications. A Fitzpatrick V patient developed leucoderma after iatrogenic melasma treatment and was treated with fractional Er:YAG and 0.01% bimatoprost. This is not evidence of efficacy or frequency; it is a reminder that treatment-induced hypopigmentation may require specialist management and may be more consequential than the original pigmentation ([Eimpunth et al., 2023](https://doi.org/10.1097/dss.0000000000003868)).

The direction of progress is therefore clear: shorter pulses, fractional delivery, multiple wavelengths, improved cooling, and image-based monitoring are being combined to widen the therapeutic window. The evidence is not yet strong enough to claim that newer necessarily means better. For several innovations, the strongest supported conclusion is that they are technically plausible and clinically promising, with small or short studies showing feasibility.

## Intense pulsed light: current applications and recent advances

### Spectrum, filtering, and mechanism

IPL systems emit a broad spectrum, commonly described as approximately 500–1200 nm. Cutoff filters remove shorter wavelengths and shape the treatment toward melanin, oxyhemoglobin, or both. The mechanism combines selective absorption by chromophores with controlled bulk heating and, in some protocols, dermal remodeling. IPL can therefore reduce erythema, superficial pigment irregularity, and some textural changes in the same treatment course.

The 2026 Lumenis M22 real-world study used 515–560-nm filters for many vascular and pigmentary indications. Fluence was individualized from 12–18 J/cm² for Fitzpatrick I–III and 10–15 J/cm² for Fitzpatrick IV, with pulse durations of 5–20 ms. The study’s endpoint was mild erythema and transient darkening of pigmented lesions, followed by cooling, moisturization, and sun avoidance ([Fan and Yu, 2026](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12833585/)).

IPL is especially sensitive to treatment context. A filter that is useful for a vascular target may not be appropriate for melasma or darker skin. Broad-spectrum light also exposes melanocytes to wavelengths that may increase pigmentation, particularly when fluence, cooling, pulse structure, or interval is poorly selected.

### IPL modality catalog

| IPL for solar lentigines | Green or KTP-like filters can concentrate energy toward superficial melanin | Lesion lightening and facial or hand photodamage | Older prospective KTP-filtered IPL evidence reported improvement with minimal downtime but declining effect over six months | Robust lesion-specific 2020–2026 clearance and recurrence data were not retrieved |

### Photoaging and multidimensional rejuvenation

A retrospective real-world study of 236 adults treated with six or more Lumenis M22 sessions provides the most substantial recent IPL dataset supplied. The population included 183 Fitzpatrick III and 53 Fitzpatrick IV participants, with acne, rosacea, and cosmetic-rejuvenation groups. In the regular-treatment group, median erythema area decreased from 640.00 to 372.40 mm², hyperpigmentation area from 577.54 to 370.61 mm², and the displayed wrinkle index from 216.60 to 95.00 after the sixth session; all pre/post comparisons were reported as statistically significant.

The study also found that regular treatment was associated with favorable response, with an odds ratio of 13.621, and that total session number was associated with response, odds ratio 3.796. Fitzpatrick IV compared with III predicted lower favorable response, odds ratio 0.121. Transient erythema and edema resolved within 48 hours, and no serious adverse events, scarring, blistering, or prolonged hyperpigmentation were reported.

These findings support IPL as a practical multidimensional rejuvenation tool, but they do not establish causal superiority. The cohort was retrospective, included several diagnoses, lacked a no-treatment or standardized comparator, and allowed clinician-specific filter and fluence adjustments. The source also contains an internal reporting inconsistency: the displayed wrinkle values imply a change from 216.60 to 95.00, whereas the prose reports a median improvement of 123.5. This does not invalidate the direction of the finding, but it limits precise interpretation ([Fan and Yu, 2026](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12833585/)).

The 2026 critical review of IPL literature classified contemporary evidence using Oxford levels and concluded that the strongest recent support lies in erythematotelangiectatic rosacea, meibomian-gland dysfunction, and selected rejuvenation protocols. Melasma, PIH, and broader aesthetic applications remain emerging because studies differ in filters, pulse structures, intervals, concomitant treatments, comparators, and endpoints ([Lee et al., 2026, IPL critical review](https://jcrm.jams.pub/article/1/2/27)).

### Solar lentigines and age spots

IPL is a routine option for solar lentigines because broad light can treat multiple lesions and associated erythema in one session. The supplied evidence, however, does not provide a robust 2020–2026 stand-alone IPL estimate for lesion-specific clearance or long-term recurrence.

A 2019 study summarized in the 2026 532-nm laser review evaluated IPL with a KTP-like filter in 16 Fitzpatrick II–III patients with facial and hand solar lentigines. Significant pigment improvement and minimal downtime were reported, but the effect gradually declined over six months. This is useful context for expected maintenance needs, but it is older, small, and not a direct comparison with a modern picosecond platform ([532-nm green laser review](https://www.mdpi.com/2079-9284/13/3/128)).

The BBL HERO plus MOXI report is more recent but does not isolate IPL. Nine patients, all Fitzpatrick II or III, received one combined treatment. BBL HERO used full-face 515- or 560-nm filters, with spot treatments in seven patients, followed by level-3 1927-nm MOXI. The report’s abstract describes a significant VISIA brown-spot improvement, but the displayed full-sample table reports baseline 21.4 versus post-treatment 34.1, mean change 12.7, p=0.11. Only the eight-patient subgroup with reduced pigmentation reached p=0.03. Follow-up varied from two weeks to 20 months, one patient maintained improvement for nearly 20 months, and another followed for approximately 19 months did not improve. No adverse events were reported. This is a hypothesis-generating combination report, not a quantitative estimate of IPL monotherapy clearance ([BBL HERO plus MOXI report](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11460752/)).

### Melasma

Stand-alone IPL for melasma remains controversial. In a prospective study of 32 Fitzpatrick IV–V patients, IPL through 640- and 690-nm filters was delivered monthly for six sessions. Of 26 completers, 12 improved, 10 were unchanged, and 4 deteriorated. MASI changed from 6.70±3.53 to 6.32±3.90, p=0.6891. Erythema and pain were common, and the authors advised against IPL as first-line treatment in darker skin, allowing use only after careful deliberation ([Choudhary et al., 2020](https://doi.org/10.2478/sjdv-2020-0001)).

This negative result does not prove that every IPL protocol fails. It does demonstrate that a broad “IPL treats melasma” claim is not transferable across phototypes, filters, fluences, and patient selection. The positive 2026 Fan–Yu cohort did not contain a melasma-specific subgroup, so its generalized reduction in hyperpigmentation cannot override the negative melasma trial.

The strongest recent IPL evidence concerns combination with a Q-switched laser. A 2026 systematic review and meta-analysis included 31 controlled studies and 2,801 adults, including 26 randomized and five nonrandomized trials. Compared with monotherapy, QS laser plus IPL produced greater MASI improvement, standardized mean difference −1.20, 95% CI −1.36 to −1.05. The pooled clinical efficacy rate was 92.0% versus 77.4%, with a relative risk of 1.10. Four studies reported recurrence of 8.5% versus 17.8%, relative risk 0.54.

The confidence in these outcomes is not uniform. GRADE rated MASI, clinical efficacy, adverse reactions, and satisfaction as moderate-quality evidence, but recurrence as low-quality because only four studies reported it. The included studies were predominantly East Asian and concentrated in Fitzpatrick III–V. The authors emphasize that at least 12 months of follow-up is needed to establish durability, whereas many studies supplied only short-term data. The pooled result supports a promising combination strategy, not a universal IPL protocol or a definitive long-term anti-recurrence effect ([QS laser plus IPL meta-analysis](https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/medicine/articles/10.3389/fmed.2026.1749950/full)).

## LED and photobiomodulation: current applications and recent advances

### Mechanism and dose

PBM uses low-irradiance red or near-infrared light to modulate cellular activity without deliberate ablation. The best-characterized photoreceptor is mitochondrial cytochrome-c oxidase, which absorbs red light near 665 nm and near-infrared light near 810 nm. Activation is associated with altered ATP production, reactive oxygen species signaling, nitric-oxide modulation, cellular proliferation, and inflammatory regulation. Fibroblasts, keratinocytes, and endothelial cells may all contribute to the clinical response ([Koperdowska, 2026, LED/PBM review](https://journals.viamedica.pl/forum_dermatologicum/article/view/111321)).

PBM has a biphasic dose response. Insufficient energy may not produce a measurable response, while excessive dose can become inhibitory through oxidative stress. The relevant variables are not only total fluence but irradiance, exposure time, wavelength, distance, treatment geometry, and repetition.

The 2026 review reports that consumer masks commonly deliver approximately 5–35 mW/cm² and 1–5 J/cm² per session, although its own summary table gives somewhat different output ranges for red and blue devices. It cites 20–60 J/cm² as a range often considered optimal for full cytochrome-c oxidase activation, but this should not be treated as a universal prescription because biological response depends on wavelength, tissue, and device geometry. Incomplete or inaccurate reporting of PBM parameters is a major barrier to cross-device comparison.

| LED/PBM approach | Wavelength and dose example | Mechanism and target | Clinical findings | Evidence and safety limits |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Red LED | Usually 630–660 nm; one home-mask study used 630±10 nm, 15.6 J/cm², 12 minutes twice weekly | Fibroblast and keratinocyte signaling, ATP and repair pathways, collagen-related remodeling | Fine wrinkles, roughness, dermal density, and tone homogeneity may improve over eight to 12 weeks | Best LED evidence is for modest photoaging improvement; studies are often small and unblinded |
| Amber PBM | About 590 nm; one randomized study used 3.8 J/cm² for 10 sessions over four weeks | Proposed cellular and collagen-related effects, less established than red PBM | Periocular wrinkle volume declined 29.9% in a 137-woman split-face trial; melasma pilot was negative and underpowered | Useful experimental rejuvenation wavelength; not established for melasma |
| Near-infrared PBM | Commonly around 810 nm; dose varies widely | Deeper mitochondrial, nitric-oxide, oxidative-stress, and inflammatory modulation | Mechanistically plausible for repair and inflammation; pigment-specific clinical evidence is sparse | Long-term pigment safety and standardized dosimetry remain uncertain |
| Green LED | 505 nm | Experimental suppression of melanogenesis pathways in cellular and 3D skin models | A human mask intervention reportedly reduced facial pigmentation | Human sample size, schedule, effect size, and durability were unavailable in the supplied report |
| Consumer red-light masks | Device-dependent, often lower output and broad beam geometry | Home PBM with variable tissue dose | AAD summarizes patient-reported improvement in wrinkles, redness, texture, and dark spots | FDA clearance indicates low public risk, not proven effectiveness; darker phototypes may develop more persistent hyperpigmentation |

### Photoaging and rejuvenation

The most informative recent red-LED study enrolled 20 healthy Caucasian volunteers, aged 45–70 years, with signs of facial aging. Participants used a 630±10-nm mask delivering 15.6 J/cm² for 12 minutes twice weekly for three months. At day 84, crow’s-foot depth decreased by 38.3%, dermal density increased by 47.7%, cheek roughness decreased by 23.8%, and complexion homogeneity improved by 34.9%. The measured changes remained at approximately the day-84 level 14 and 28 days after treatment stopped. These results suggest a measurable short-term structural and optical effect, but the study had only 20 participants, no comparator, and allowed usual skincare and makeup throughout. The authors also disclosed relationships with the device company ([Couturaud et al., 2023](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10311288/)).

A larger split-face randomized trial included 137 women aged 40–65 years with Fitzpatrick II–IV skin and Glogau II–IV photoaging. Participants received 10 sessions over four weeks, with 660-nm red PBM on one side and 590-nm amber PBM on the other, both at 3.8 J/cm². Periocular wrinkle volume decreased by 31.6% with red light and 29.9% with amber light. Neither treatment improved hydration or viscoelasticity, although quality-of-life questionnaires improved. This is stronger comparative evidence for wrinkle volume than for dermal remodeling, and it does not establish long-term maintenance ([red and amber PBM trial](https://sage.cnpereading.com/doi/10.1089/photob.2022.0114)).

The 2026 PBM review also summarizes a study of 31 participants who received nine LED sessions. Reported improvements included periorbital wrinkles, elasticity, smoothness, and firmness, with more than half of participants rating improvement at 25–50%. The treatment was well tolerated, but direct collagen measurement and long-term follow-up were not reported in the review summary ([Koperdowska, 2026](https://journals.viamedica.pl/forum_dermatologicum/article/view/111321)).

The American Academy of Dermatology summarizes one facial red-light study in which 90 patients received eight treatments over four weeks; more than 90% reported some improvement, including softer and smoother skin, less redness, and lightening of dark spots. The AAD cautions that differing devices, treatment durations, and study designs prevent direct comparison and that more research is needed to determine optimal dosing and maintenance ([AAD red-light guidance](https://www.aad.org/public/cosmetic/safety/red-light-therapy)).

### Brightening and pigmentary outcomes

LED studies reporting “complexion homogeneity,” “luminosity,” “dark-spot lightening,” or melanin-index changes do not establish generalized whitening. A more even complexion may reflect reduced erythema, reduced focal pigmentation, improved optical uniformity, or altered hydration and surface reflection.

The 505-nm green-LED work is a notable recent development but remains preliminary. In B16 mouse melanoma cells and three-dimensional skin models, 505-nm light reduced microphthalmia-associated transcription factor and tyrosinase expression and reduced melanin without affecting cell viability. A human facial-mask intervention also reportedly decreased pigmentation. However, the supplied human report gives no sample size, treatment schedule, numerical effect size, or durability. The appropriate classification is mechanistic and early clinical evidence, not an established depigmentation treatment ([Mima et al., 2025/2026 version](https://doi.org/10.2340/actadv.v105.43441)).

### Melasma and darker skin

No high-quality randomized clinical evidence establishes LED or PBM as an effective treatment for melasma. A 2025 double-blind randomized pilot trial compared active amber PBM with placebo cream against sham PBM with 5% liposomal tranexamic-acid cream for 12 weeks. Only 21 women were randomized, 10 to PBM and 11 to tranexamic acid. MASI and physician global assessment did not differ significantly within or between groups. The study ended early with only 51% statistical power, so it cannot exclude a modest effect, but it cannot establish efficacy. PBM caused warmth; tranexamic acid caused burning, and transient increased pigmentation occurred in the tranexamic-acid group at week six ([Galache et al., 2025](https://www.springermedicine.com/tranexamic-acid/melasma/amber-led-photobiomodulation-versus-tranexamic-acid-for-the-trea/51214274)).

The pigmentary risk of visible light is clinically important. The 2026 PBM review reports that 400–700-nm exposure produced darker and more persistent pigmentation in Fitzpatrick IV–VI than UVA1, with pigment persisting up to 14 days and a dose response. The effect was absent in phototype II. On that basis, the review advises caution or avoidance of visible-light LED therapy in melasma, particularly in darker phototypes, and recommends visible-light-inclusive photoprotection.

This creates an important disagreement between marketing-oriented claims and clinical caution. The 2023 red-mask study states that its design allowed inclusion of phototypes V and VI without risk, but the cohort and design were not adequate to establish long-term pigment safety in those groups. The AAD likewise warns that darker skin tones are more sensitive to visible red light and may develop more intense and longer-lasting hyperpigmentation. Red light may be safe for many users in the short term, but “non-UV” does not mean “pigment-neutral” for every patient.

### LED safety and practical role

Short-term adverse effects are generally mild: warmth, transient pain, irritation, dryness, or erythema. LED devices do not normally produce the crusting, blistering, or prolonged wound care associated with ablative resurfacing. Their low downtime is a major practical advantage.

Safety is nevertheless dependent on wavelength, output, eye protection, photosensitivity, and the treated person’s pigment biology. The AAD recommends dermatologist review for people with photosensitive conditions such as lupus, those taking photosensitizing medication, and those who need device-specific eye protection. It also emphasizes that FDA clearance means the device is considered low risk, not that its effectiveness has been proven.

For aesthetic medicine, the most defensible role of LED/PBM is adjunctive or maintenance-oriented treatment for mild photoaging, barrier recovery, and selected inflammatory or reparative goals. It should not replace diagnosis and treatment of melasma or focal pigmented lesions, and it should not be marketed as a validated generalized whitening method.

## Photoaging and skin brightening outcomes

### What improves most reliably

Across modalities, the best-supported photoaging outcomes are reduction in fine wrinkles, roughness, pores, mottled pigmentation, and visible erythema. The relative strength of each modality depends on whether the primary target is texture, focal pigment, diffuse dyschromia, or vascular change.

A 2025 split-face trial comparing fractional 1064-nm picosecond Nd:YAG with fractional Q-switched 1064-nm Nd:YAG illustrates the importance of separating within-treatment improvement from between-device superiority. Thirty participants with Fitzpatrick III–IV skin received five sessions at weeks 0, 2, 4, 6, and 8. At three months after the final session, wrinkle counts fell from 84.53±25.75 to 52.17±26.11 on the picosecond side and from 89.43±25.22 to 50.23±22.18 on the Q-switched side. Pores, texture, and histologic collagen and elastic-fiber organization also improved. None of the between-modality differences in wrinkles, pores, texture, semi-quantitative score, or GAIS was statistically significant. The trial supports comparable photoaging efficacy, not a proven picosecond advantage ([Tang et al., 2025](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12210001/)).

Histology showed increased collagen and improved elastic-fiber alignment on both sides. More pronounced collagen proliferation on the picosecond side was described, but only three participants underwent biopsy and the difference was not statistically significant. Histologic remodeling is therefore a plausible mechanism, not a validated reason to promise superior clinical collagen stimulation.

A 2026 double-blind split-face trial of one 1064-nm picosecond session followed by eight weeks of a multifunctional serum provides a different kind of evidence. Twenty-four women aged 30–48 years received the same laser on both sides, followed by serum on one side and placebo on the other. At day 57, the serum side had a 25.0% higher efficacy rate for overall photoaging assessment and a 20.83% higher efficacy rate for fine wrinkles. Melanin index fell 10.45% from baseline on the serum side versus 5.13% on the placebo side. The result supports an aftercare effect in a small, short trial; it does not isolate the laser’s independent contribution or support generalized whitening ([He et al., 2026](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13144715/)).

### Objective versus subjective improvement

Objective tools increasingly shape aesthetic studies, but they measure different constructs:

- VISIA quantifies image-derived erythema, pigmentation, pores, or wrinkles using proprietary indices.
- Chromametry measures color coordinates or differences between facial sites.
- Melanin meters estimate optical melanin content.
- PRIMOS or similar systems measure wrinkle volume or area.
- Cutometry measures deformation and elastic recovery.
- Ultrasound estimates dermal density.
- Reflectance confocal microscopy visualizes cellular and structural patterns.
- Histology can demonstrate collagen, elastin, melanocyte, or melanin changes in biopsied skin.

These endpoints cannot be assumed interchangeable. A lower VISIA pigment index may represent fewer visible spots, reduced contrast, or altered image characteristics; it is not automatically equivalent to a percentage reduction in melanin. A patient’s satisfaction may improve without a large MASI change, or an objective index may improve without a corresponding perceived benefit.

The QS-plus-IPL meta-analysis demonstrates this distinction. Objective MASI and clinical efficacy favored combination treatment, but patient satisfaction did not differ significantly. The authors attribute this possible divergence to expectations, fear of relapse, transient treatment effects, and the limited sensitivity of simple satisfaction scales. A high-quality clinical assessment should therefore include both standardized objective measures and validated patient-reported outcomes.

### Collagen and tissue remodeling

The mechanistic rationale for collagen remodeling is strongest for fractional thermal injury and red/NIR PBM. Fractional 1550- and 1927-nm studies report increased collagen, elastic fibers, and hyaluronic acid. Fractional 1064-nm picosecond and Q-switched studies show histologic collagen and elastin organization. Red and amber PBM studies report wrinkle-volume reduction, while the biological rationale invokes fibroblast activation and mitochondrial signaling.

Direct clinical evidence of collagen quantity remains sparse. Many studies infer remodeling from histology, ultrasound density, wrinkle reduction, or texture changes. These measures should be reported separately. A visible improvement in wrinkle volume is clinically meaningful even if direct collagen quantification is unavailable, but it should not be described as proof that a specific device produces a defined amount of new collagen.

### Timing and durability

Treatment speed is highly protocol-dependent:

- A pigment-selective 532-nm laser may visibly alter a discrete lentigo after one session, but short-term clearance does not establish permanence.
- Fractional photoaging treatment typically requires a series of sessions, with improvement developing over weeks as epidermal renewal and dermal remodeling occur.
- IPL commonly requires repeated treatments; the 2026 real-world cohort associated regular intervals and more sessions with better outcomes.
- LED/PBM generally requires repeated home or clinic sessions over four to 12 weeks and maintenance treatments.
- Melasma improvement may appear within one to three months but often declines after treatment stops.

The best supplied durability data are heterogeneous. The red LED mask study observed persistence at 14 and 28 days after stopping. The combined long-pulse 1064 plus picosecond 755-nm trial reported GAIS benefits at three and six months. The 1064-nm melasma trial followed participants to week 24, but all used intensive sunscreen. The dual-mode melasma trial followed patients for 12 months and showed that an early relapse difference disappeared by six and 12 months. These results support maintenance rather than a one-time cure model.

### Brightening is not generalized whitening

The available clinical literature supports four narrower claims:

1. Visible dark spots or mottled pigmentation may decrease.
2. Uneven facial tone may become more uniform.
3. Erythema may decline, making the complexion appear brighter.
4. Melanin-index or chromametric values may improve in treated areas.

It does not support a claim that lasers, IPL, or LED safely and predictably lighten a person’s overall natural skin color. The distinction is clinically important because generalized whitening language can encourage excessive treatment, obscure PIH or hypopigmentation, and reinforce ethically problematic color hierarchies. Aesthetic documentation should identify the lesion or endpoint being treated and should state whether the outcome is objective, subjective, calculated, or hypothetical.

## Hyperpigmentation: solar lentigines versus melasma

The two conditions should not be combined into one “pigmentation” category. Their biology, treatment goals, risk-benefit balance, and durability are different.

| Feature | Solar lentigines or age spots | Melasma | Clinical consequence |
|---|---|---|---|
| Typical appearance | Discrete, sharply demarcated macules on sun-exposed skin | Symmetric patches, commonly on the cheeks, forehead, upper lip, or jaw | Lesion-selective treatment is more straightforward for lentigines |
